items.title: Integral symmetric Jucys–Murphy polynomials span the center
items.statement: For every commutative unital ring $R$ and $n\ge0$, every element of $Z(RS_n)$ is an $R$-linear combination of evaluations of integral monomial symmetric polynomials at $L_r=\sum_{a<r}(a,r)$. Conversely every symmetric polynomial evaluation is central. In particular $Z(RS_n)=R[L_1,\ldots,L_n]^{\mathrm{sym}}$, where the right side denotes evaluations of symmetric polynomials, not invariants of an action on the group algebra. No integer is inverted.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $n\ge0$, a commutative unital ring $R$, and the Jucys–Murphy elements.

[F1] The elements $L_r$ commute ([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]); every symmetric polynomial evaluation over $\mathbb C$ is central ([[thm-symmetric-polynomials-in-jucys-murphy-elements-give-the-center]]). Only the centrality direction over $\mathbb C$ is used.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 An integral symmetric polynomial evaluates in $\mathbb ZS_n$. Its commutator with any permutation vanishes in $\mathbb CS_n$ by [F1], hence vanishes integrally by coefficientwise injectivity. For any coefficient ring, invariance of a polynomial under variable permutations says exactly that its coefficients are constant on monomial orbits, so it is a linear combination of integral monomial symmetric polynomials. All their evaluations are therefore central over $R$. A group-ring element is central exactly when its coefficients are constant on conjugacy classes: compare coefficients after conjugating by each permutation. Consequently the class sums form a basis of the center over $\mathbb Z$ and over $R$, even with zero divisors. [F1, given, algebra]

1.2 Define the reduced cycle type $\rho(g)$ by subtracting one from each nontrivial cycle length and discarding fixed points. Its size $d(g)=n-c(g)$ is the minimum number of transpositions expressing $g$: multiplying by a transposition changes the number of cycles by one, giving the lower bound, and each cycle of length $s$ has a factorization with $s-1$ transpositions, giving equality. The possible types are precisely partitions $\rho$ with $|\rho|+\ell(\rho)\le n$. Write $K_\rho$ for their integral class sums. [given, algebra]

2.1 If a word of $d$ transpositions has product of degree $d$, every prefix multiplication joins two different cycles; otherwise the final degree would be at most $d-2$. The graph whose edges are the transpositions is therefore a forest, and its connected components are exactly the cycles of every prefix product. Indeed initially both are singletons, and each multiplication joins two current components by one edge and joins their two cycles. Thus edges never repeat, and each final tree of $s$ vertices gives a cycle of length $s$. [step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Let $\rho$ be a possible reduced type of size $d$, and expand the monomial symmetric polynomial $m_\rho(L_1,\ldots,L_n)$, summing once over distinct assignments of the positive parts of $\rho$ to distinct indices $r$. Each term is a word of $d$ transpositions, grouped into stars centered at those $r$: the group $L_r^a$ has $a$ edges incident to $r$. Every resulting permutation has degree at most $d$. If its degree is $d$, step 2.1 makes all these stars trees with distinct edges. Each star lies in one final tree; the degree of that tree is the sum of the exponents of its stars. Its reduced cycle type is therefore obtained from $\rho$ by merging some parts. Any proper merging decreases the number of parts. [step 2.1, F1, algebra]

4.1 The coefficient at any permutation $g$ of reduced type exactly $\rho$ is one. In the degree-$d$ expansion, equality of the number of parts forces each final tree to contain exactly one star. For a cycle with support $\{r,a_1,\ldots,a_s\}$, the center of its star must be its largest letter $r$, since every factor from $L_r$ is $(a,r)$ with $a<r$. The ordered star factorization is unique: with right-to-left permutation composition, $(a_1,r)\cdots(a_s,r)$ is the cycle $(r,a_s,\ldots,a_1)$, as direct evaluation on each letter shows. Thus the cycle determines the leaf ordering. Different cycles have distinct maxima, their stars are disjoint and commute, and their assignments appear exactly once among the distinct monomials, including repeated exponents. This also constructs a term producing $g$. [step 3.1, step 2.1, algebra]

5.1 By centrality and steps 3.1–4.1, $m_\rho(L)=K_\rho+\sum_\sigma a_{\rho\sigma}K_\sigma$, with integer coefficients, where every remaining type either has smaller degree or is a proper merging of $\rho$. Induct on degree and, within a degree, on the number of parts in increasing order. All remaining sums are already integral symmetric polynomial evaluations, so subtraction expresses $K_\rho$ that way too. The initial type is empty with $m_\varnothing=K_\varnothing=1$. This proves integral spanning without division. Specialization to $R$ and the class-sum basis from step 1.1 prove the assertion over every $R$, including $n=0$ and the zero ring. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Generalized Jucys-Murphy primary idempotents and the residue-summand functors $E_i$, $F_i$
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). Write $\mathcal C_n=(\mathbb F_p)^n/S_n$ for the set of content classes
(equivalently, multisets of $n$ residues). For $\alpha\in\mathcal C_n$ let
$I_\alpha$ be the set of sequences representing $\alpha$, and put
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 14), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves centrality, idempotency, orthogonality, primitivity and
exhaustiveness locally; the residue functors use the first three properties.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content class
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i\in\mathbb F_p,\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$, with the sum indexed by $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$, put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 *Eigenvalues in $\mathbb F_p$.* Let $h_r\in\mathbb Q[X]$ be the minimal polynomial of $L_r$ acting on the left regular module $\mathbb QS_n$. Over $\mathbb C$ the regular module is the direct sum of the complex Specht modules with multiplicities, and by [F2] the eigenvalues of $L_r$ on that module are the integers $c_T(r)$, the contents of the node containing $r$, over all standard tableaux $T$ of $n$ nodes; hence $h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-a)$ is squarefree with the integer roots in the finite set $E_r$. The group-basis coordinates of $h_r(L_r)$ are integers and vanish over $\mathbb Q$, so this identity holds already in $\mathbb ZS_n$. Reduction of coefficients modulo $p$ therefore gives $h_r(L_r)=0$ in $kS_n$, so the minimal polynomial $f_r$ of $L_r$ on the regular module $kS_n$ divides the reduction $\bar h_r=\prod_{a\in E_r}(X-\bar a)$ in $k[X]$, and every root of $f_r$ lies in the image $\mathbb F_p$ of $\mathbb Z$ in $k$. [F2, F9, given, algebra]

1.2 *Antipode invariance.* The antipode $\sigma:kS_n\to kS_n$, $\sigma(g)=g^{-1}$, is an anti-automorphism fixing every transposition, hence fixes each $L_r$ and therefore each $P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]$ and each $e(\mathbf i)$. [given, algebra]

1.3 *An integral central identity.* In $\mathbb ZS_n$ one has $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{c(g)}g$, where $c(g)$ is the number of cycles, including fixed points. To prove this by induction, regard $S_{n-1}$ as fixing $n$. A term multiplied by $u$ leaves $n$ fixed and adds one cycle. A term multiplied by $(a,n)$ inserts $n$ in the cycle containing $a$, without changing its cycle count. Conversely, deleting a nonfixed $n$ from its cycle uniquely recovers the permutation in $S_{n-1}$ and the transposition used. Thus every permutation occurs exactly once. Comparing coefficients, each elementary symmetric polynomial $C_s$ in $L_1,\ldots,L_n$ is a sum of all permutations with $n-s$ cycles and hence is central; the identity and centrality remain true after reduction to $k$. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 *Primary projectors.* Write $f_r=\prod_{a\in\mathbb F_p}(X-a)^{m_a}$ with $m_a\ge0$. For $a\ne b$ the ideals $\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ and $\big((X-b)^{m_b}\big)$ of $k[X]$ are comaximal, since two powers of distinct linear polynomials are coprime and Bezout gives $1=u(X)(X-a)^{m_a}+v(X)(X-b)^{m_b}$. By [F4] applied to the ring $k[X]/(f_r)$ and its comaximal ideals, the canonical map $k[X]/(f_r)\to\prod_{a:m_a>0}k[X]/\big((X-a)^{m_a}\big)$ is an isomorphism; let $\varepsilon_{r,a}$ be the preimage of the idempotent supported at the $a$-th factor when $m_a>0$, and put $\varepsilon_{r,a}=0$ when $m_a=0$. Then $\sum_a\varepsilon_{r,a}=1$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}^2=\varepsilon_{r,a}$, $\varepsilon_{r,a}\varepsilon_{r,b}=0$ for $a\ne b$, and $(X-a)^{m_a}\varepsilon_{r,a}=0$ in $k[X]/(f_r)$. Substituting the algebra element $L_r$ for $X$ (legitimate because $f_r(L_r)=0$) gives elements $P_{r,a}:=\varepsilon_{r,a}(L_r)\in k[L_r]$ with $\sum_aP_{r,a}=1$, $P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a}$ and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}P_{r,a}=0$. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 *These are the primary projections.* Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module. Since the $P_{r,a}$ are polynomials in $L_r$, they commute with $L_r$ and with one another; as $1=\sum_aP_{r,a}$ one has $M=\sum_aP_{r,a}M$, and $(L_r-a)^{m_a}$ annihilates $P_{r,a}M$, so $P_{r,a}M\subseteq M_{r,a}$. Conversely, if $m\in M_{r,a}$, then $(L_r-a)^Nm=0$ for $N\ge m_a$, and for $b\ne a$ the element $L_r-b=(a-b)+(L_r-a)$ is invertible on the $a$-primary subspace because $(a-b)\in k^\times$ and $(L_r-a)$ is nilpotent there; from $P_{r,b}(L_r-b)^{m_b}=0$ we get $P_{r,b}m=0$ for $b\ne a$, whence $m=P_{r,a}m$. Thus $P_{r,a}M=M_{r,a}$ and $M=\bigoplus_aM_{r,a}$. The products $e(\mathbf i)=\prod_rP_{r,i_r}$ are idempotent, pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$ by multiplicativity of the $P_{r,a}$; applying the same argument successively to the commuting operators $L_1,\dots,L_n$ gives $e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$. [step 2.1, F1, algebra]

4.1 *Central CRT separates contents.* Choose $N\ge1$ such that $(L_r-i_r)^Ne(\mathbf i)=0$ for every $r$ and every tuple $\mathbf i$, using step 2.1 and the finiteness of the indices. On the commutative algebra summand $e(\mathbf i)k[L_1,\ldots,L_n]$ with identity $e(\mathbf i)$, the commuting elements $(L_r-i_r)e(\mathbf i)$ generate an ideal whose $D$-th power is zero for $D=n(N-1)+1$: every monomial of degree $D$ has a factor with exponent at least $N$. Thus $C_s-c_s(\mathbf i)$ belongs to that nilpotent ideal, where $c_s(\mathbf i)$ is the elementary symmetric function of the residues. The tuple $c(\mathbf i)=(c_1(\mathbf i),\ldots,c_n(\mathbf i))$ determines the content, because $\prod_r(X-i_r)=\sum_{s=0}^n(-1)^sc_s(\mathbf i)X^{n-s}$ determines the multiplicities of its distinct linear factors, over every characteristic. In $R=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]$, the distinct content tuples therefore define distinct pairwise comaximal maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_\alpha=(Y_s-c_s(\alpha):1\le s\le n)$; their powers $\mathfrak m_\alpha^D$ are also pairwise comaximal, since expanding $1=(a+b)^{2D-1}$ for $a+b=1$ places every term in one of the two $D$-th powers. By [F4], choose $Q_\alpha\in R$ congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak m_\alpha^D$ and to $0$ modulo every other $\mathfrak m_\beta^D$. The nilpotence just proved gives $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)e(\mathbf i)=e(\mathbf i)$ when $\mathbf i\in I_\alpha$, and $0$ otherwise. Since the tuple idempotents sum to $1$, it follows that $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)=e_\alpha$. This is central by step 1.3. Idempotency, pairwise orthogonality for distinct content classes, and $\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal C_n}e_\alpha=1$ follow from step 3.1 and the partition of all tuples into their content classes. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.3, algebra]

5.1 *The functor projectors.* Fix $i\in\mathbb F_p$ and $\alpha\in\mathcal C_{n-1}$. The primary projectors for $L_r$, $r<n$, computed in $kS_{n-1}$ agree with those in $kS_n$: the primary idempotents in $k[L_r]$ are uniquely determined by their congruences modulo the powers of the distinct linear factors of the minimal polynomial, and the inclusion preserves the polynomial relations of $L_r$. Summing once over each distinct sequence representing $\alpha$ gives $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i))=e_\alpha^{(n-1)}P_{n,i}$. By step 4.1 the first factor is central in $kS_{n-1}$, while the second commutes with $kS_{n-1}$ by [F1]; their product is therefore an idempotent commuting with that subgroup algebra. The sets $\{(\mathbf j,i):\mathbf j\in I_\alpha\}$ are disjoint for distinct pairs $(\alpha,i)$ and partition all tuples of length $n$. Consequently these idempotents are pairwise orthogonal and sum to $1$, and their images are $kS_{n-1}$-submodules. Grouping these actual direct summands by the last residue gives $\operatorname{Res}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb F_p}E_iM$. The indexing is by content classes throughout, so no content is counted twice. [step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, F1, F5, algebra]

5.2 *Every nonzero content summand has local center.* Fix $e=e_\alpha\ne0$. Since $e$ is central, $Z(e kS_n)=eZ(kS_n)$: an element central in the summand commutes with the complementary summand because their products vanish. By [F7] every element of this center is $ef(L)$ for a symmetric polynomial $f$ over $k$. For every $\mathbf i\in I_\alpha$, the difference $(f(L)-f(\mathbf i))e(\mathbf i)$ belongs to the nilpotent ideal of step 4.1; symmetry makes $f(\mathbf i)$ the same scalar $a=f(\alpha)$ for all these tuples. The orthogonal sum of these differences is nilpotent with the common exponent $D$ of that step. Hence every central element of the summand has the form $ae+u$ with $u$ nilpotent. The scalar $a$ is unique: a nonzero scalar multiple of $e$ is invertible in this nonzero summand and cannot be nilpotent. As the center is commutative, sums of commuting nilpotents and their products with any central element are nilpotent. Thus its nilpotents form an ideal, the scalar map is a surjective ring homomorphism onto $k$, and every element with nonzero scalar is invertible by the finite geometric series. The center is local over the original field $k$, without extending scalars. [step 4.1, F7, algebra]

6.1 *Induction side.* The same computation with $n$ replaced by $d+1$ shows that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_{d+1}$ commuting with $kS_d$, that $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$ with pairwise orthogonal summands, and that $kS_{d+1}=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$; hence for any finite-dimensional $M$, $$kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M=\bigoplus_{i,\alpha}kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M=\bigoplus_iF_iM,$$ the middle step using $M=\bigoplus_\alpha e_\alpha M$ and the centrality of $e_\alpha$ in $kS_d$. This is $\operatorname{Ind}M=\bigoplus_iF_iM$. [step 4.1, step 5.1, F5, algebra]

6.2 *Primitivity and exhaustiveness.* A central idempotent $b$ in $e kS_n$ has scalar $0$ or $1$ by step 5.2. In the first case $b$ is nilpotent and idempotent, so $b=0$; in the second case $e-b$ is nilpotent and idempotent, so $b=e$. Thus each nonzero $e_\alpha$ is primitive central. Their orthogonal sum is $1$ by step 4.1. Any primitive central idempotent $b$ of $kS_n$ decomposes as $\sum_\alpha be_\alpha$ into orthogonal central idempotents; primitivity leaves exactly one nonzero term, and the primitivity of that $e_\alpha$ forces $b=e_\alpha$. By [F6] these are precisely the block idempotents. At rank zero $kS_0=k$ and $e(\varnothing)=1$ gives the unique block; restriction from rank zero is taken to be the zero functor, while induction to rank one has only residue $0$. This convention does not invoke a group $S_{-1}$. [step 5.2, step 4.1, F6, algebra]

7.1 *Exactness and duality.* Each $E_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$; a map $f:M\to N$ of $kS_n$-modules commutes with the action of the element $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, so it restricts to a map $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M\to e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}N$, and each such functor is exact as a direct summand of the identity, hence additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. Each $F_i$ is a direct sum of the functors $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$, which are direct summands of induction $M\mapsto kS_{d+1}\otimes_{kS_d}M$; by [F5] $kS_{d+1}$ is free as a right $kS_d$-module, so induction, and with it each $F_i$, is exact, additive and finite-dimensionality preserving. For duality observe that $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is fixed by the antipode by step 1.2, and that the standard nondegenerate pairing $M\times M^*\to k$ satisfies $(xm,f)=(m,x^*f)$; hence for finite-dimensional $M$ the transpose of the projection on $M$ is the projection on $M^*$ and $(e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M)^*\cong e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M^*$, giving $E_i(M)^*\cong E_i(M^*)$. All these restriction-duality identifications are $k$-linear and natural. [step 1.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, F5, algebra]

7.2 *Induction duality by a perfect coset pairing.* Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $\pi_H:kG\to kH$ retain the coefficients of the elements of $H$. For a finite-dimensional left $kH$-module $M$, with contragredient action $(a f)(m)=f(a^{-1}m)$, define $\langle g\otimes m,h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}g)m)$ between $\operatorname{Ind}M$ and $\operatorname{Ind}M^*$. For $a\in H$, the $kH$-bimodule property of $\pi_H$ gives $\pi_H(h^{-1}ga)=\pi_H(h^{-1}g)a$ and $\pi_H((ha)^{-1}g)=a^{-1}\pi_H(h^{-1}g)$; these identities prove balancing in the first and second tensor factors, respectively. Simultaneous left multiplication of $g,h$ by any element of $G$ leaves $h^{-1}g$ unchanged, proving $G$-invariance. On a finite left-coset transversal $T$ one has $\pi_H(s^{-1}r)=\delta_{s,r}1$ for $r,s\in T$. Thus the pairing is the direct sum of the perfect evaluations $M\times M^*\to k$ and is perfect by [F5]. For $e=e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$, right multiplication $R_e(g\otimes m)=ge\otimes m$ is a well-defined $G$-linear idempotent because $e$ commutes with $kH$. Let $\tau:kG\to k$ be the coefficient of $1$; directly on group elements, $\tau(xy)=\tau(yx)$. For every $b\in H$, the coefficient of $b$ in $ze$ equals $\tau(b^{-1}ze)=\tau(eb^{-1}z)=\tau(b^{-1}ez)$, since $e$ commutes with $b$. Therefore $\pi_H(ze)=\pi_H(ez)$ for all $z\in kG$. Writing $e^*$ for its antipode image, step 1.2 gives $e^*=e$, so expansion in the group basis yields $\langle R_e(g\otimes m),h\otimes f\rangle=f(\pi_H(h^{-1}ge)m)=f(\pi_H(eh^{-1}g)m)=\langle g\otimes m,R_e(h\otimes f)\rangle$. The two images of $R_e$ pair perfectly: a vector in either image annihilating the other annihilates the entire opposite space, since the opposite kernel is orthogonal to that image, and hence vanishes by perfectness. By tensor balancing, $ge\otimes m=ge\otimes e_\alpha m$, so these images are precisely $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M$ and $kG e\otimes_{kH}e_\alpha M^*$. Distinct $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ images are orthogonal by self-adjointness and projector orthogonality. Summing the perfect image pairings over $\alpha\in\mathcal C_d$ proves the natural $G$-isomorphism $F_i(M^*)\cong F_i(M)^*$; invariance supplies the contragredient action, and evaluation shows naturality in $M$. The construction uses finite transversals and holds over every characteristic, including $2$. [step 1.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, F5, algebra]

8.1 *Partition content agrees with the block content.* Let $\lambda\vdash n$ and let $\alpha$ be the multiset of its node contents reduced modulo $p$. Over $\mathbb C$, [F2] makes every elementary symmetric $C_s$ act on $S^\lambda$ by the integer $c_s(\lambda)$. In the integral basis of [F8] the matrix of $C_s-c_s(\lambda)$ has integer entries and vanishes after tensoring with $\mathbb C$, so it vanishes integrally and after specialization to $k$. Thus the CRT polynomial $Q_\alpha(C_1,\ldots,C_n)$ of step 4.1 acts as $1$ on $S^\lambda_k$, while the other content projections act as zero. The same is true on its nonzero subquotients. Hence any simple module obtained from this Specht module belongs to the block $e_\alpha$, establishing the stated content dictionary without a splitting-field descent or a reduced interpolation denominator. [F2, F8, step 4.1, step 6.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Residue signatures, normal, good, conormal and cogood nodes
items.statement:
Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence, after deleting the zero entries, a terminal word is
$+^a-^b$ for some $a,b\ge0$; cancelled positions remain in their original
places and need not form a contiguous block. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. Uniqueness follows
by induction on the number of nonzero entries. A terminal word admits no
step. Otherwise, two distinct first steps commute and reach a common word
after one further step each. All these successor words have fewer nonzero
entries, so the induction hypothesis identifies their terminal words. Thus
any two reduction sequences have the same terminal word; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has the unique addable node $(1,1)$, of residue $0$,
and no removable nodes. Its $0$-signature is $(+)$ and its other signatures
are empty. Thus $\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=0$ for every $i$,
$\varphi_0(\varnothing)=1$, and $\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for $i\ne0$.
It has no good node and its cogood $0$-node is $(1,1)$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).
items.strategy: Finite termination and commuting disjoint reductions imply unique terminal word by induction on the number of nonzero entries, as proved in the Definition. Cancelled positions need not be contiguous; deleting zeros gives +^a-^b. Empty has unique addable residue0 node(1,1), signature+, epsilon_i=0, phi_0=1 and phi_i=0 for i nonzero; no good node and cogood0=(1,1).

items.title: Finite-group induction is coinduction, hence biadjoint to restriction
items.statement:
Let $H\le G$ be finite groups and let $k$ be any field. For every left
$kH$-module $M$ the map
$$\Phi_M:\ \operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=kG\otimes_{kH}M\longrightarrow\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{kH}(kG,M),\qquad \Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x)=\begin{cases}(xg)m,&xg\in H,\\ 0,&xg\notin H,\end{cases}$$
is a natural isomorphism of $kG$-modules
([[def-restriction-induction-and-coinduction-for-group-modules]]). Consequently
$\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\cong\operatorname{Coind}_H^G$ naturally, so induction
is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction
([[thm-induction-is-left-adjoint-and-coinduction-right-adjoint-to-restriction]])
and is exact. No hypothesis on the characteristic of $k$, on splitting
fields, or on the prime $2$ is needed, and the argument is choice-free: it
uses only the finite selection of least representatives of the finitely many
left cosets.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite groups $H\le G$, a field $k$, a left $kH$-module $M$, and a
set $T\subseteq G$ containing exactly one representative of each left coset
$gH$ (a left transversal), chosen as the set of least elements for a fixed
linear order of $G$.

[F1] $\operatorname{Ind}_H^GM=kG\otimes_{kH}M$ is the tensor product of the
$(kG,kH)$-bimodule $kG$ with $M$, with $g\cdot(x\otimes m)=gx\otimes m$; the
elements of $kG$ form a $k$-basis, and the defining relations are
$xh\otimes m=x\otimes hm$ for $h\in H$. The coinduced module
$\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM=\operatorname{Hom}_{kH}(kG,M)$ consists of the
$k$-linear maps $\varphi$ with $\varphi(hx)=h\varphi(x)$ for all $h\in H$,
$x\in G$, with $(g\varphi)(x)=\varphi(xg)$
([[def-restriction-induction-and-coinduction-for-group-modules]]).

[F2] Induction is left adjoint and coinduction is right adjoint to
restriction ([[thm-induction-is-left-adjoint-and-coinduction-right-adjoint-to-restriction]]).

[F3] $kG$ is free as a right $kH$-module on any left transversal, so
$kG\otimes_{kH}-$, that is induction, preserves exactness; a
supplied transversal is the only choice input
([[lem-the-group-ring-is-free-over-a-subgroup-ring]]).

[F4] Every element of $G$ is uniquely $th$ with $t\in T$, $h\in H$, and
$G$ is the disjoint union of the cosets $gH$, $g\in G$; $H$ is a finite group
and every product in $kG$ is a finite sum.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 $\Phi_M$ is a well-defined $kG$-linear map. For fixed $g,m$ the formula defines a function on $G$: if $xg\in H$ then $(xg)m\in M$, otherwise $0$. It is $k$-linear in $x$ by definition, and it is $kH$-linear: for $h\in H$ and $x\in G$, $\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(hx)=((hx)g)m$ if $hxg\in H$ and $0$ otherwise; since $hxg=(hx)g$ and $hxg\in H\iff xg\in H$ (as $h,h^{-1}\in H$), this equals $h((xg)m)=h\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x)$ in the first case and $0$ in the second. Hence $\Phi_M(g\otimes m)\in\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM$. The map is $k$-linear and in the second tensor variable balanced: for $h\in H$, the functions $\Phi_M(gh\otimes m)$ and $\Phi_M(g\otimes hm)$ both send $x$ to $((xg)h)m=(xg)(hm)$ when $xg\in H$ and to $0$ otherwise; so $\Phi_M$ is well defined on the tensor product. Finally it is $kG$-linear: $\Phi_M(g_0g\otimes m)(x)=((xg_0)g)m$ if $xg_0g\in H$ and $0$ otherwise, and $(g_0\Phi_M(g\otimes m))(x)=\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(xg_0)=((xg_0)g)m$ if $xg_0g\in H$ and $0$ otherwise, the two conditions being the same. [given, F1]

1.2 The inverse on coinduced maps. For $\varphi\in\operatorname{Coind}_H^GM$, define $\Psi_M(\varphi)=\sum_{t\in T}t\otimes\varphi(t^{-1})$. This is a finite sum and a $k$-linear map. Inverting the left cosets $tH$ shows that the right cosets $Ht^{-1}$ partition $G$. If a representative is replaced by $t'=th$ with $h\in H$, then $t'\otimes\varphi(t'^{-1})=th\otimes\varphi(h^{-1}t^{-1})=th\otimes h^{-1}\varphi(t^{-1})=t\otimes\varphi(t^{-1})$, by $kH$-linearity and the balancing relation. Thus the inverse formula is independent of the finite transversal. [given, F1, F4]

2.1 $\Phi_M\Psi_M=\mathrm{id}$. For $x\in G$, there is exactly one $t_0\in T$ for which $x\in Ht_0^{-1}$, equivalently $xt_0\in H$. Write $x=ht_0^{-1}$. Then $\Phi_M(\Psi_M(\varphi))(x)=\sum_{t\in T,\ xt\in H}(xt)\varphi(t^{-1})=h\varphi(t_0^{-1})=\varphi(x)$, using the right-coset partition from step 1.2 and $kH$-linearity. Equality on the group basis gives equality on $kG$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F4]

2.2 $\Psi_M\Phi_M=\mathrm{id}$. For $g\in G$ and $m\in M$, write uniquely $g=t_0h$ with $t_0\in T$ and $h\in H$. Then $\Psi_M(\Phi_M(g\otimes m))=\sum_{t\in T,\ t^{-1}g\in H}t\otimes(t^{-1}g)m=t_0\otimes hm=g\otimes m$, by the left-coset partition and tensor balancing. Since such elementary tensors span the induced module, this proves the second inverse identity. [step 1.1, step 1.2, F1, F4]

3.1 Naturality and consequences. If $f:M\to M'$ is a $kH$-map, then for all $g,m,x$ one has $\Phi_{M'}(g\otimes f(m))(x)=f(\Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x))$, because the formula is evaluated by multiplication in $M$ or $M'$ and $f$ is linear; hence $\Phi$ is a natural transformation, and by steps 2.1 and 2.2 each $\Phi_M$ is an isomorphism with natural inverse $\Psi_M$. Therefore $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\cong\operatorname{Coind}_H^G$ as functors, and [F2] yields that induction is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction: the left adjunction is its induction adjunction, and the right adjunction is transported across this natural isomorphism from the coinduction adjunction. Induction $kG\otimes_{kH}-$ is right exact, and coinduction $\operatorname{Hom}_{kH}(kG,-)$ is left exact; a natural isomorphism between the two functors therefore makes induction exact, in agreement with the freeness of $kG$ over $kH$ recorded in [F3]. No hypothesis on $k$, on characteristic, or on splitting is used, and the only selection made is the finite transversal $T$ of least representatives. [step 2.1, step 2.2, F2, F3] ∎

## Remarks

- **Freyd's adjoint functor heuristics.** The isomorphism is the finite-group
  relative Frobenius map; it is the reason the modular branching page can use
  the biadjunction of restriction, and the two adjunctions are *not*
  identified by hand: the right adjunction is obtained by transporting the
  coinduction adjunction along $\Phi$.
- **Finiteness of $G/H$ is what is used.** The argument needs the finiteness
  of $T$ in step 1.2 and the total vanishing of all but one term in steps 2.1
  and 2.2; for infinite $G/H$ these fail in general. The finite transversal
  is selected by least elements, so no choice principle enters.

items.title: The socle of an uncoloured modular restriction is the multiplicity-free sum over the good residues
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted
partition of $d\ge1$; write $D(\mu)$ for the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
Let $A_i$ denote the good $i$-node of $\mu$, for those
$i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i),$$
a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules: distinct residues give
distinct summands. The sum runs over the residues $i$ with
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, one good node per such residue; the completely
reducible special case (the restriction is semisimple if and only if every
normal node is good, Kleshchev II Theorem 0.6) is a separate statement and is
not asserted here.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 By [F1] the restriction decomposes as $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iD(\mu)$ with each $E_iD(\mu)$ a $kS_{d-1}$-submodule, and by [F5] the socle of the restriction is the direct sum $\bigoplus_i\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))$. [given, F1, F5]

1.2 By the local restriction argument [F3], for each residue $i$ the module $\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))$ is $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$ and is $0$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; by [F3] each $\mu\setminus A_i$ is a $p$-restricted partition of $d-1$, so each displayed $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ is a simple $kS_{d-1}$-module by [F4]. [given, F3, F4]

2.1 Summing the descriptions of step 1.2 over the finitely many residues $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and using step 1.1 gives $$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i).$$ [step 1.1, step 1.2, F3]

3.1 The sum is multiplicity-free and its summands are pairwise non-isomorphic: if $i\ne j$ and both $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varepsilon_j(\mu)$ are positive, then the good nodes $A_i$ and $A_j$ have different residues and are therefore distinct nodes of $\mu$, so the $p$-restricted partitions $\mu\setminus A_i$ and $\mu\setminus A_j$ of $d-1$ are distinct by [F2]; by [F4] their simple modules $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ and $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ are non-isomorphic. Each residue contributes its summand once, so each isomorphism class occurs with multiplicity one in the displayed socle. [step 2.1, F2, F4]

4.1 The displayed decomposition of step 2.1 has the left-hand side $\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}(D(\mu)\downarrow_{S_{d-1}})$ and, by step 3.1, is a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules with one summand per residue $i$ satisfying $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$. No claim is made here about the restriction being semisimple. In the smallest case $d=1$ one has $\mu=(1)$, and the only node of residue $0$ is the removable node $(1,1)$, so $\varepsilon_0(\mu)=1$ and the right-hand side is the single term $D(\varnothing)=k$, while the restriction to the trivial group $S_0$ is $k$ itself, in agreement with the display; this is the smallest instance in which the summands carry the empty partition as a label. [step 2.1, step 3.1, given] ∎

items.title: Good-node deletion and cogood-node addition operators
items.statement:
On the set of $p$-restricted partitions
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]) define partial operators
$\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]), the
operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most
one cogood node exist in each residue. No module-theoretic statement is made
here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A prime $p$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$, and $p$-restricted partitions $\mu,\nu$ of ranks $d$ and $d-1$.

[F1] For a $p$-restricted partition $\lambda$ the $i$-signature is the word in $\{+,-\}$ read off the addable and removable $i$-nodes ordered top to bottom, and its reduced form, after deleting zero entries, $+^a-^b$ is well defined; the good $i$-node of $\lambda$ is the removable node of the first surviving $-$, the cogood $i$-node is the addable node of the last surviving $+$, and $\varepsilon_i(\lambda),\varphi_i(\lambda)$ are the numbers of surviving $-$ and $+$ signs ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]).

[F2] Let $\lambda$ be $p$-restricted and $X=(r,\lambda_r)$ a removable $i$-node. On deleting $X$, only boundary nodes in rows $r-1,r,r+1$ can change. A newly removable node in row $r-1$ occurs only when $\lambda_{r-1}=\lambda_r$, and has residue $i+1$; a newly removable node $(r,\lambda_r-1)$ has residue $i-1$. The former row-$r$ addable node has residue $i+1$. A row-$(r+1)$ addable node is lost only when $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}=1$, and then has residue $i-1$. These residues are different from $i$ for every prime $p\ge2$. Thus the only change to an $i$-boundary node is that $X$ changes from removable to addable: $\operatorname{Rem}_i(\lambda\setminus X)=\operatorname{Rem}_i(\lambda) \setminus\{X\}$ and $\operatorname{Add}_i(\lambda\setminus X)= \operatorname{Add}_i(\lambda)\cup\{X\}$. This follows directly from the row inequalities in [[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]; it does not assert that every boundary node in row $r+1$ is retained.

[F3] The reduction of a signature word is confluent, and the zero-suppressed normal form $+^a-^b$ can be computed by scanning the word from left to right, pushing each non-cancelled $-$ on a stack and letting each $+$ cancel the top $-$ of the stack if the stack is nonempty, and surviving otherwise; the surviving signs in their original order are exactly the normal form ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]).

[F4] If $\lambda$ is a partition and $X$ a removable node of $\lambda$, then $\lambda\setminus X$ is a partition, and $\lambda\cup Y$ is a partition for every addable node $Y$ of $\lambda$; the restricted condition compares the consecutive differences $\lambda_a-\lambda_{a+1}$ with $p$ ([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], [[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 *The stack algorithm computes the normal form.* The stack algorithm of [F3] terminates with a word containing no $-$ before a $+$ (a surviving $-$ stays on the stack and blocks the stack from being empty, so no later $+$ survives after it), and the reduction relation is confluent by [F3], so the surviving signs read in order are the reduced signature with zero entries deleted, $+^a-^b$; in particular the good node corresponds to the first surviving $-$ and the cogood node to the last surviving $+$. [given, F3]

1.2 *Comparison of the $i$-words.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and $X$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$; put $\nu:=\mu\setminus X$. By [F2] the $i$-nodes of $\nu$ are obtained from those of $\mu$ by removing $X$ from the removable list and inserting $X$ into the addable list, all other $i$-nodes and their top-to-bottom order being unchanged; hence the $i$-signature words of $\mu$ and $\nu$ have the same length and the same entries except at the position $p$ of $X$, where the word of $\mu$ has $-$ and the word of $\nu$ has $+$. [given, F2]

2.1 *First surviving $-$ versus last surviving $+$.* Let $w$ be a signature word with $w_p=-$, let $w'$ be $w$ with the entry at $p$ changed to $+$, let $u$ be the prefix of $w$ strictly before $p$, and let $s$ be the suffix strictly after $p$. We prove that $p$ is the position of the first surviving $-$ of $w$ if and only if $p$ is the position of the last surviving $+$ of $w'$. Let $S$ be the stack of [F3] after scanning $u$; the prefix of $w'$ before $p$ is the same word $u$, so the same stack $S$ is present there. If $S$ is nonempty, let $q$ be its bottom entry; scanning $w$ further, $q$ can leave the stack only by being cancelled by a $+$ that has first cancelled every entry above it, in particular the entry at $p$, so either $q$ survives, giving a surviving $-$ before $p$, or the entry $p$ is cancelled before $q$ and does not survive; in both cases $p$ is not the first surviving $-$ of $w$. Similarly, scanning $w'$ the entry at $p$ is a $+$, which survives only if the stack just before it is empty, so if $S$ is nonempty then $p$ does not survive and is not the last surviving $+$ of $w'$. Hence both events force $S$ to be empty, and we may assume this. With $S$ empty, push the $-$ at $p$ in the scan of $w$; while this entry is alive, the pending entries above it after scanning a prefix $q$ of $s$ are the $-$ signs of $q$ not yet cancelled, and since no $+$ has yet occurred at height $0$, that number is $\#-(q)-\#+(q)$. Consequently $p$ is cancelled at the first $+$ of $s$ whose preceding prefix $q$ has $\#+(q)=\#-(q)$, and such a $+$ exists if and only if some prefix $q$ of $s$ has $\#+(q)>\#-(q)$: counts change by one at each symbol, so a strict surplus arises only across a step of equality, and conversely a prefix with equality followed by a $+$ would create a strict surplus. Thus, with $S$ empty, the entry at $p$ survives in $w$ if and only if $$(C)\quad \#+(q)\le\#-(q)\quad\text{for every prefix }q\text{ of }s.$$ In $w'$, the $+$ at $p$ arrives at the empty stack $S$ and survives; after it, a later $+$ of $s$ survives exactly when the stack is empty at its arrival. If (C) holds and a $+$ of $s$ survived, with preceding prefix $q$, then all $-$ of $q$ were cancelled, so $\#-(q)\le\#+(q)$, while (C) applied to the prefix $q$ extended by that $+$ gives $\#+(q)+1\le\#-(q)$, a contradiction; hence no later $+$ survives. Conversely, if (C) fails then some $+$ of $s$ survives: the stack height after a prefix $q$ of $s$ equals $\#-(q)-\#+(q)+c(q)$, where $c(q)$ is the number of $+$ signs of $q$ that survived, as one checks by induction on the length of $q$ (a $-$ raises the height, and a $+$ raises $c$ by one and lowers the height by one exactly when it cancels); if no $+$ of $s$ survived then $c(q)=0$ for every prefix $q$, so $\#+(q)\le\#-(q)$ for every prefix, contradicting the failure of (C). Therefore (C) holds if and only if, in $w'$, the entry at $p$ is the last surviving $+$, and the claim follows. [step 1.1, F3]

3.1 *Good versus cogood for a removable node.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted, $X$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ and $\nu=\mu\setminus X$. By step 1.2 the words of $\mu$ and $\nu$ differ exactly by the flip at the position of $X$, so step 2.1 gives: $X$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$ if and only if $X$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\nu$. Consequently, if $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$ and $X$ is the good $i$-node, then $\varphi_i(\nu)>0$ with cogood node $X$, and $\tilde f_i(\nu)=\nu\cup X=\mu$. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1]

3.2 *Removing the good node preserves restrictedness.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and let $A=(r,\mu_r)$ be its good $i$-node; we show that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$ is $p$-restricted. If $r\ge2$ and $\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r=p-1$, then $B:=(r-1,\mu_{r-1})$ is a removable node of $\mu$ (as $\mu_{r-1}>\mu_r$) with $\operatorname{res}(B)=\mu_{r-1}-(r-1)=\mu_r-r+p\equiv\mu_r-r=\operatorname{res}(A)$, so $B$ is a removable $i$-node above $A$ and hence occurs before $A$ in the $i$-word. There is no $i$-node between $B$ and $A$: these are consecutive rows, and any addable node in either row has residue $i+1$. Thus $B$ is still on the stack when $A$ is pushed. Either some $-$ before $A$ survives, and then $A$ is not the first surviving $-$, or every $-$ before $A$ is eventually cancelled, in particular $B$; but a $+$ cancels $B$ only after cancelling every entry pushed after $B$, in particular the entry at $A$, so in that case $A$ is cancelled and does not survive; both alternatives contradict that $A$ is good. Hence $\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r\le p-2$, and then $\nu$ is $p$-restricted: deleting the last node of row $r$ leaves $(\mu_r-1)-\mu_{r+1}\le p-2<p$ and, if $r\ge2$, $\mu_{r-1}-(\mu_r-1)=(\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r)+1\le p-1<p$, while all other consecutive differences are unchanged. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F4, given]

3.3 *Adding the cogood node preserves restrictedness.* Let $\mu$ be $p$-restricted and let $B=(r,\mu_r+1)$ be its cogood $i$-node; we show that $\nu=\mu\cup B$ is $p$-restricted. Suppose first that $\mu_r-\mu_{r+1}=p-1$; then $D:=(r+1,\mu_{r+1}+1)$ is an addable $i$-node of $\mu$, because $\mu_r>\mu_{r+1}$ and $\operatorname{res}(D)=\mu_{r+1}-r\equiv\mu_r+1-r=\operatorname{res}(B)$; between $B$ and $D$ in the top-to-bottom order there is no $i$-node: the entries after $B$ in row $r$ do not exist, and the remaining $i$-node of row $r$ is the removable node $(r,\mu_r)$, whose residue is $\operatorname{res}(B)-1$, while the addable node of row $r+1$ is $D$ itself. Hence $B$ and $D$ are consecutive in the $i$-word, both with sign $+$. If the $+$ at $B$ survives, it leaves the stack empty, so the next entry, the $+$ at $D$, also survives and is later than $B$; if the $+$ at $B$ does not survive, then $B$ is not the cogood node. In both cases $B$ is not the last surviving $+$, contradicting that $B$ is cogood. Hence $\mu_r-\mu_{r+1}\le p-2$, and then $(\mu_r+1)-\mu_{r+1}\le p-1<p$, while $\mu_{r-1}-(\mu_r+1)=(\mu_{r-1}-\mu_r)-1<p$ for $r\ge2$ (no row above change is needed when $r=1$), and all other differences are unchanged; so $\nu$ is $p$-restricted. [step 1.2, step 2.1, F4, given]

4.1 *Good versus cogood for an addable node.* Let $Y$ be an addable $i$-node of $\mu$ and $\nu:=\mu\cup Y$. The node $Y$ is removable in $\nu$, and $\mu=\nu\setminus Y$; applying step 3.1 to the pair $(\nu,Y)$ gives: $Y$ is the good $i$-node of $\nu$ if and only if $Y$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$. Consequently, if $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$ and $Y$ is the cogood $i$-node, then $\varepsilon_i(\nu)>0$ with good node $Y$, and $\tilde e_i(\nu)=\nu\setminus Y=\mu$. [step 3.1, F1]

5.1 *The inverse property.* Let $\mu,\nu$ be $p$-restricted partitions. If $\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$, then $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, $\nu=\mu\setminus A$ for the good $i$-node $A$ of $\mu$, and step 3.1 gives that $A$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\nu$, so that $\tilde f_i\nu=\nu\cup A=\mu$. Conversely, if $\mu=\tilde f_i\nu$, then $\varphi_i(\nu)>0$, $\mu=\nu\cup B$ for the cogood $i$-node $B$ of $\nu$, and step 4.1 gives that $B$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$, so that $\tilde e_i\mu=\mu\setminus B=\nu$. Hence $\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\iff\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$ for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$, both sides being false when the relevant node does not exist; and by steps 3.2 and 3.3 the operators map $p$-restricted partitions to $p$-restricted partitions. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, step 4.1]

6.1 *Conclusion.* By [F1] at most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node exist in each residue, so the partial operators are well defined; removing a node lowers the rank by one and adding a node raises it by one, so $\tilde e_i$ lowers and $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one; and by step 5.1 each operator is defined at exactly the images of the other, so they are mutual inverses on their domains. No module theory and no choice principle are used. [step 5.1, F1] ∎
## Remarks

- **The word comparison is where the geometry enters.** Step 1.2 is the only place where the partition structure is used; the reduction of a *general* word does not behave this way, so the inverse property is a theorem about the $i$-words of partitions, not a formal property of the cancellation procedure.
- **One-sided cancellation.** The reduction cancels only $-+$ pairs, so a reduced word may contain both a surviving $+$ before a surviving $-$, as in the reduced signatures $(+,-)$ appearing on the companion page.
- **Choice.** Everything is finite and explicit; no choice principle is used.

items.title: Every $p$-restricted partition is reached from the empty partition by cogood additions
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Every $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$ is obtained from the empty partition by $d$ successive cogood
additions: there are residues $i_1,\dots,i_d$ with
$$\mu=\tilde f_{i_d}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing;$$
equivalently, every $p$-restricted $\mu\ne\varnothing$ has at least one good
node, and successive good deletions carry $\mu$ to $\varnothing$
([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]],
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Hence, in
the graph whose vertices are the $p$-restricted partitions and whose edges
join $\nu$ to $\tilde f_i\nu$ for every $i$ for which the operator is
defined, the empty partition is the unique vertex of rank $0$ and every
vertex is reached from it; dually every vertex reaches the empty partition by
successive good deletions. The argument is choice-free.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Restriction is faithful on nonzero modules. Let $M\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module and consider the multiplication map $\varphi:kS_d\otimes_{kS_{d-1}}M\to M$, $\varphi(g\otimes m)=gm$, where $M$ is regarded as a $kS_{d-1}$-module by restriction. It is $kS_d$-linear and surjective, since the image of $1\otimes m$ is $m$ and the elements $m$ span $M$; hence if the restriction of $M$ to $kS_{d-1}$ were zero, the tensor product would be zero and $M=0$, a contradiction. Therefore restriction sends no nonzero module to zero. [given, F1]

1.2 Nonzero finite-dimensional modules have nonzero socle: choosing a nonzero submodule of least positive dimension gives a simple submodule, so the socle, which is the sum of all simple submodules, is nonzero. [given, F2]

1.3 $D(\mu)$ is a nonzero simple $kS_d$-module by [F3], because $\mu$ is $p$-restricted. [given, F3]

2.1 Applying step 1.1 to $M=D(\mu)$ with $d\ge1$: since $D(\mu)\ne0$ by step 1.3, its restriction to $S_{d-1}$ is nonzero. [step 1.1, step 1.3]

3.1 By step 1.2 applied to the nonzero finite-dimensional $kS_{d-1}$-module $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)$ from step 2.1, the socle $\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}(D(\mu)\downarrow_{S_{d-1}})$ is nonzero. [step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 By the residue-refined socle theorem [F4], the socle is the multiplicity-free sum of the simple modules $D(\mu\setminus A_i)$ over the residues $i$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$. Since this socle is nonzero by step 3.1, at least one residue satisfies $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$. [step 3.1, F4]

5.1 Fix such a residue $i$. By [F5] the good $i$-node $A_i$ exists, $\nu:=\mu\setminus A_i$ is a $p$-restricted partition of $d-1$, and $\mu=\tilde f_i\nu$ with $\tilde f_i\nu=\nu\cup A_i$. [step 4.1, F5]

6.1 Induction on $d$. We prove that every $p$-restricted partition of $d$ is reachable from $\varnothing$ by $d$ cogood additions. For $d=0$ the empty partition is the only partition and it is reached by the empty sequence. For $d\ge1$ and a $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ of $d$, if $\mu=\varnothing$ there is nothing to prove, and otherwise step 5.1 supplies a residue $i$ and a $p$-restricted partition $\nu$ of $d-1$ with $\mu=\tilde f_i\nu$; by the inductive hypothesis $\nu=\tilde f_{i_{d-1}}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing$ for suitable residues, whence $\mu=\tilde f_i\tilde f_{i_{d-1}}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing$. The residue $i$ is selected as, say, the least residue with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, so no choice principle is used. [step 5.1, induction]

7.1 Good deletions carry every $p$-restricted partition to $\varnothing$. At each nonempty stage step 5.1 produces a good node and, by [F5], the partition obtained by deleting it is again $p$-restricted of rank one less; iterating $d$ times reaches the only partition of rank $0$, which is $\varnothing$; equivalently, by the inverse property in [F5], the two procedures are mutually inverse step by step. [step 6.1, F5]

8.1 Consequences for the graph. By definition the edges of the graph are the partial operations $\nu\mapsto\tilde f_i\nu$, so step 6.1 says exactly that every $p$-restricted partition is reached from $\varnothing$; step 7.1 says every vertex reaches $\varnothing$ by good deletions $\tilde e_i$. The empty partition is the unique partition of $0$, so it is the unique rank-$0$ vertex, and it has no incoming edge from a $p$-restricted partition because no partition of $-1$ exists; all ranks are finite. No step used the characteristic of $k$ beyond the existence of the socle theorem [F4], and no choice principle was used. [step 6.1, step 7.1] ∎

items.title: The crystal identification does not elementarily identify the cellular simple labels
items.statement:
Two labellings of the simple modules of the group algebra $kS_d$ and of the
Hecke algebra $H_d$ are in play on this page and on the Fock-space page.

- The **cellular labels** $D(\mu)=\operatorname{hd}(S(\mu))$ are the heads of
  the Specht modules in the dual-Specht convention; they are the labels used
  by the modular classification
  ([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
- The **inductive (crystal) labels** $\dot D(\mu)$ are defined recursively
  from the residue-summand functors $F_i$ of
  [[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] by
  $\dot D(\varnothing)=k$ and, for $\mu\ne\varnothing$,
$$\dot D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(F_i\dot D(\tilde e_i\mu)\bigr) \quad\text{for any }i\text{ for which }\tilde e_i\mu\text{ is defined},$$ the
  operators $\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ being those of
  [[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]] and the independence
  of the choice of $i$ a theorem of the crystal theory. The two labellings
  agree, $$\dot D(\mu)\cong D(\mu)\qquad(\mu\ \text{p-restricted}),$$ and this
  identification (11.1) of Kleshchev's survey is *not* elementary: it was
  first established by Ariki and later by graded arguments, both depending on
  the full theory of the cyclotomic Hecke/KLR categorification.

Consequently no proof on this page or on the later Fock-space page may use
Fock-space reachability to establish the cellular classification of simple
modules, or the cellular classification to establish the Fock-space
component; the two directions are separated by this reminder. In particular
the socle theorem
`cor-socle-of-uncoloured-modular-restriction-is-the-sum-over-good-residues`
and the branching theorems of this page are stated and used for the cellular
labels, while any statement about the crystal operators as operators on Fock
space is a separate obligation of the Fock-space page.
items.strategy:
## Remarks

- **Why the identification is not formal.** The definition of $\dot D(\mu)$
  uses only the functors $F_i$ and the already-constructed simple modules of
  smaller rank, whereas $D(\mu)$ is the head of an explicit Specht module;
  the equality of the two families is a strong statement about the
  categorification, not a consequence of the combinatorial inverse property
  of the operators.
- **The direction used here.** Only the cellular labels are assigned
  module-theoretic meaning on this page; the symbol $\dot D(\mu)$ occurs on
  the Fock-space page, where the identification is available through the
  cited theorem.

For the group-algebra specialization, the cellular endpoint statement
[[thm-cogood-node-gives-the-simple-socle-and-head-of-residue-induction]]
and the reachability argument
[[prop-every-p-restricted-partition-is-reached-by-cogood-node-additions]]
give a precise conditional comparison without using Fock-space
classification. Induct on rank. At rank zero both labels are $k$. For any
allowed predecessor $\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$, the combinatorial inverse property
gives $\tilde f_i\nu=\mu$. If the lower-rank inductive label is $D(\nu)$,
the cellular cogood theorem makes the head of $F_iD(\nu)$ the simple
$D(\mu)$. Thus every allowed choice of $i$ produces this same simple module.
Reachability ensures at least one predecessor. This argument is conditional
on the actual cellular endpoint proof and its suppliers, and supplies no
general-Hecke functor or endpoint theorem. Kleshchev's cited comparison
concerns the broader cyclotomic setting; its non-elementary proof history
does not make this rank induction a proof of that broader theorem.

items.title: An integral essential-subset basis and count for type-A root intervals
items.statement:
Let $F$ have characteristic $p>0$, let $N\ge2$, and let $\mu=(\mu_1\ge\cdots\ge\mu_N\ge0)$ be a polynomial highest weight. Let $L_N(\mu)$ be the nonzero Schur Weyl-cell simple at $q=1$, regarded as a left module by star, with its canonical highest vector $v$. Put $a_i=\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}$. For every $1\le r\le s<N$, define $B(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^j a_t$ and $C(i,j)=j-i+\sum_{t=i}^{j-1}a_t$, reduced modulo $p$ for zero tests. A matching is an injection $d$ with $x\le d(x)$; it need not preserve order between different sources. Call $J\subseteq(r,s]$ essential when no $t<u$ outside $J$ in $[r,s+1]$ admits a zero-$B$ matching $\{t\}\cup(J\cap(t,u))\to[t,u)$. Write $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$ for the number of essential sets.

The vectors $T_{r,s}(J)v$ constructed by the explicit integral coefficient recursion in the proof, indexed by essential $J$, form a basis of $L_N(\mu)_{\mu-\alpha_r-\cdots-\alpha_s}$. In particular this weight-space dimension is $\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, including dimension zero. The construction has integer-polynomial coefficients, and its positive-word pivots remain valid in every field of characteristic $p$.

Define a root $x$ to be normal in $[x,y]$ when $a_x\ne0$ and its demands $m>x$ with $B(x,m)=0$ admit an injection $z$ satisfying $x<z(m)\le m$ and $B(z(m),m)=0$. If $r$ is not normal set $\nu_a(r,s)=0$; otherwise let it be the number of $x\in[r,s]$ normal in $[x,s]$ with $C(r,x)=0$. Set $\varepsilon'_a(r,t)=\varepsilon_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$, where only coordinate $t$ is increased by one. Then, as ordinary integers,
$$\varepsilon_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^s\varepsilon'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s).$$
No restrictedness condition is imposed on $\mu$ or on the shifted auxiliary highest weights.
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Extend only to $K=F(t)$. This field is infinite, and extension preserves the rank of every finite Gram matrix. A nonzero Schur cell-form quotient stays simple after this extension: in any field a vector outside its radical generates the entire cell module by the cellular rank-one action, and the same argument applies to the extended nonzero Gram form. No algebraic closure or infinite-choice step is required. [F1, F2, construct]

2.1 At $q=1$, identify $\bigoplus _\nu M^\nu$ with the tensorword basis of $(K^N)^{\otimes m}, m=|\mu |$, by sending $m_\nu T_{d}$ to the word whose $j$th letter is the row containing entry $j$ in the row-standard tableau $t^\nu d$. This is the explicit right-coset/tensorword convention; for regular type and basis $d$, that letter is $j d^{-1}$ under right permutation notation. The symmetric-group action on tensor positions is transported through this map, so inverses in labels and right-position actions are fixed consistently. The symmetric group permutes the tensor positions. An endomorphism commuting with this permutation action has matrix coefficients constant on its orbits on pairs of words. Such orbits are indexed by nonnegative integer matrices $A=(A_{ab})$ with $\sum A_{ab}=m$, recording the number of positions with input $b$ and output $a$. Let $E_{A}$ be the matrix with entry 1 on that orbit and 0 elsewhere. The $E_{A}$ have disjoint support and form a basis of the endomorphism algebra. For a matrix $g$, $g^{\otimes m}=\sum _{A} (\prod _{ab} g_{ab}^{A_{ab}})E_{A}$. The transpose involution sends $E_{A}$ to $E_{A^T}$; it is precisely the $q=1$ Schur star (the corresponding semistandard Hom maps are transposes under the orthonormal tensorword/permutation forms). [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Invertible-matrix evaluations span this Schur algebra over $K$. Indeed a linear functional annihilating all $g^{\otimes m}$ gives a polynomial $P(g)=\sum _{A} c_{A} g^A$ vanishing whenever $\det(g)\ne 0$. Then $P\det$ vanishes at every matrix over $K$. An elementary induction on the number of variables shows that a polynomial over an infinite field vanishing everywhere is zero: regard it as a polynomial in the last variable and use infinitely many values, then apply the induction to its coefficients. Thus $P\det=0$ as a polynomial, and the polynomial domain gives $P=0$, so all $c_{A}$ vanish. Finite-dimensional duality proves the spanning claim. Consequently the star-converted Schur simple is a simple rational left $\operatorname{GL}_N$-module, with the same submodules and composition multiplicities as the right Schur module. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The canonical semistandard tableau has weight $\mu$ and Schur form value 1. Indeed its diagonal Schur basis element is the projection onto the permutation summand $M^\mu $: the defining Hom map is the identity there and zero on the other summands. Its square is itself, so the defining cell-product coefficient, which is the canonical tableau norm, is 1. This argument uses the canonical diagonal projection only, not an idempotence assertion for all diagonal tableau elements. Every semistandard tableau weight $\nu$ is dominated by $\mu $: for each $k$, all entries $\le k$ occur in the first $k$ rows by column strictness, so there are at most $\mu _{1}+\cdots +\mu _{k}$ of them. The unique tableau of weight $\mu$ is the canonical one. Thus $L$ has highest weight $\mu$ with one-dimensional highest space $K v$, and its positive upper unipotent group fixes $v$: any nonconstant positive-root coefficient would have weight strictly above $\mu$. Torus weights are integer characters, distinct as Laurent monomials over $K$; no Lie-eigenvalue congruence substitutes for weight equality. [step 3.1, construct]

5.1 On the open set where leading principal minors are nonzero, Gaussian elimination gives $g=u^- d u^+$. The negative-unipotent coefficient operators on $v$ span $L$. To see this, let $W$ be their span and let $\ell$ annihilate $W$. Then $\ell (gv)=0$ on that open set because $u^+v=v$ and $dv$ is a scalar multiple of $v$. A polynomial matrix coefficient vanishing there vanishes identically by the same polynomial-identity argument, so $\ell$ annihilates the coefficient orbit of $v$ under all $\operatorname{GL}_{N}$. That orbit spans $L$ by simplicity. Hence $W=L$. [step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\mu -\gamma$. If they all had zero highest coefficient on $x$, the Gaussian factorization would imply that the highest coefficient of $gx$ was zero on the same open set: negative operators cannot raise a weight to $\mu$, and no weight exceeds $\mu$. The resulting polynomial identity would make that coefficient zero on the whole simple-module orbit of $x$, which spans $L$ and contains $v$, a contradiction. Thus some positive coefficient operator of weight $\gamma$ raises $x$ to a nonzero multiple of $v$. [step 5.1, construct]

7.1 For $\gamma =\alpha (r,s)$, every simple-root coefficient is 1. In a product expansion of a unipotent matrix, any monomial of total root weight $\gamma$ therefore has each root-variable exponent $0$ or $1$, and its roots are pairwise disjoint intervals covering $[r,s]$. They are exactly cut partitions of that interval. Put  $f_{a,b}=E_{b+1,a}, e_{i}=E_{i,i+1}, Y_{r,s}(U)=f_{r,u_{1}-1}f_{u_{1},u_{2}-1}\cdots f_{u_{k},s}$, for $U=\{u_{1}<\cdots <u_{k}\}\subset (r,s]$, with $Y(\varnothing )=f_{r,s}$. These words span the required negative coefficient space. Similarly the positive coefficient space is spanned by words using each $e_{r},\cdots ,e_{s}$ once. Root-matrix commutators expand every longer positive root into such simple words. Permutations of these simple letters are identified using $e_{i} e_{j}=e_{j} e_{i}$ for $|i-j|>1$; their relative orders on adjacent pairs determine the canonical representative  $Q_{r,s}(I)=e_{i_{k}}\cdots e_{i_{1}} \cdot \prod _{j\in [r,s]\setminus I}^{\mathrm{increasing}}e_{j}, I=\{i_{1}<\cdots <i_{k}\}\subset (r,s]$. Every word is carried to this representative by exchanging adjacent incomparable letters in the corresponding path partial order. Hence these $Q$ words span all positive tests at the interval weight. There are no divided powers greater than 1 or factorial denominators in this grade. [step 6.1, construct]

8.1 The actions and all commutator calculations below use $[E_{ab},E_{cd}]=\delta _{bc} E_{ad} -\delta _{da} E_{cb}, e_{i} v=0$, and $(E_{ii} -E_{i+1,i+1})v=a_{i} v$. They are integral matrix identities and apply to the actual Schur module. The construction descends from $K$ to $F$ because the resulting matrices have entries in $F$ and scalar extension preserves all ranks and linear relations. [step 7.1, construct]

9.1 For $M,U\subset (r,s]$, define $\zeta _{r,s}(M,U)$ recursively. For $M=\varnothing , \zeta (\varnothing ,U)=\prod _{j\in (r,s]\setminus U} C(r,j)$. For $M\ne \varnothing$ let $m=\min M$ and $M'=M\setminus \{m\}$. If $m\notin U$, put  $\zeta (M,U)=\zeta (M',U)/C(r,m)$. If $m\in U$, put  $\zeta (M,U)=[\zeta (M',U)-\zeta _{r,m-1}(\varnothing ,U\cap (r,m)) \zeta _{m,s}(M',U\cap (m,s])]/C(r,m)$. Every division here is performed in the integer polynomial ring before specialization. It is exact. To prove this, induct on $|M|$, keeping the stronger statement that $\zeta (M,U)=\zeta _{r,m-1}(\varnothing ,U\cap (r,m))P(C(r,m))$, where $P$ is an integer polynomial in the remaining differences independent of $r$ and of $U\cap (r,m)$. At the next smallest cut, use $C(r,j)=C(r,m)+C(m,j)$. If $m\notin U$, the numerator contains the explicit factor $C(r,m)$. If $m\in U$, the two terms are respectively evaluations $P(C+D)$ and $P(D)$, multiplied by the same left factor, with $C=C(r,m)$; their difference is divisible by $C$, since  $(C+D)^h-D^h=C \sum _{a=1}^h \binom{h}{a}C^{a-1}D^{h-a}$. This gives the stronger factorization at the next step. The base case is the displayed product. Thus all coefficients are integer polynomials even when their displayed denominators vanish modulo $p$. [step 8.1, construct]

10.1 Define  $T_{r,s}(M)=\sum _{U} \zeta _{r,s}(M,U)Y_{r,s}(U)$. The coefficient recursion is equivalently the exact negative-word recursion  $C(r,m)T_{r,s}(M)=T_{r,s}(M')-T_{r,m-1}(\varnothing )T_{m,s}(M')$.          $(T)$ This follows by separating cut words according to whether the cut $m$ occurs. Products of adjacent interval words concatenate with the boundary cut present; this is exactly the cut-word product in the numerator. [step 9.1, construct]

11.1 The following splitting identity is integral:  $T_{r,i-1}(E)T_{i,s}(F) =T_{r,s}(E\cup F)-T_{r,s}((E\setminus \{e\})\cup \{i\}\cup F)-C(e,i)T_{r,s}(E\cup \{i\}\cup F), (P)$ where $E\subset (r,i), F\subset (i,s], e=\max E$. If $E=\varnothing$ omit the middle term and set $e=r$. For $E=\varnothing$ this is $(T)$ rearranged at cut $i$. For nonempty $E$, remove its smallest $m$, insert $(T)$ on the left and apply the induction to the two shorter products. Use $C(r,i)=C(r,m)+C(m,i)$. The terms containing the extra cut $m$ cancel in pairs, and the remaining numerator is  $C(r,m)[T(E\cup F)-T((E\setminus \{e\})\cup \{i\}\cup F)-C(e,i)T(E\cup \{i\}\cup F)]$. Exact divisibility already proved permits cancellation in the integer polynomial ring; reduction to $F$ is made only afterwards. This proves $(P)$ by induction, including the singleton $E$ case.
