## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$, a removable $i$-node $A=(r,\mu_r)$ with $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
$p$-restricted, and the residue-summand functor $E_i$.

[F1] $\operatorname{Res}^{S_d}_{S_{d-1}}M=\bigoplus_jE_jM$, and $E_jM$ is the
sum of the generalized eigenspaces of the last Jucys-Murphy element
$L_d=T_d-T_{d-1}$ with eigenvalue $j$, for every finite-dimensional
$kS_d$-module $M$; here $T_m=\sum_{1\le a<b\le m}(a\ b)$ is the
transposition class sum of $S_m$
([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]],
[[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]).

[F2] The central transposition class sum $T_m$ acts on the ordinary integral Specht lattice and every field specialization by the total content $z_\xi=\sum_{(r,c)\in[\xi]}(c-r)$ ([[lem-transposition-class-sum-acts-on-a-specht-module-by-total-content]]). At $m=0,1$, both the class sum and total content are zero directly. The actual same-shape perfect pairing identifies the Murphy cell $C_{\mathrm M}(\xi)$ with the star dual of the ordinary Specht module ([[thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual]]). Since $T_m^*=T_m$, the same scalar acts on that dual and its nonzero form quotient $D(\xi)$. This uses the ordinary module itself, not a false ordinary/Murphy equality of form radicals.

[F3] For a $p$-restricted $\nu$, the module $D(\nu)$ is nonzero, simple,
self-dual and absolutely irreducible, so every $kS_{d-1}$-endomorphism of
$D(\nu)$ is a scalar ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).

[F4] The complete locally proved piecewise count is [[thm-kleshchev-first-level-branching-multiplicity]]. For the ordinary regular label $\lambda=\mu'$ and the transposed removable node $A'$, its multiplicity is zero off normality and counts the same-residue normal nodes weakly above $A'$ on normality. The group sign/conjugate dictionary and signature order in [F5] transport this exact count; no bibliographic normal-node theorem is a proof premise.

[F5] The dictionary between the two conventions: transposing exchanges
removable nodes of $\lambda$ with removable nodes of $\lambda'$, exchanges
"strictly above" for the dual order of the same residue class, and negates
residues, $c-r\mapsto r-c$; the normal nodes of $\lambda'$ in the signature
sense are exactly the transposes of the normal nodes of $\lambda$ in
Brundan's sense ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Localization of an occurring factor. On $D(\mu)$ the class sum $T_d$ acts by $z_\mu$ by [F2], hence it acts by that scalar on the whole restriction. The operator $L_d=T_d-T_{d-1}$ on this restriction is therefore $z_\mu-T_{d-1}$, a central $kS_{d-1}$ operator preserving every submodule. If $D(\nu)$ occurs as a composition factor, [F2] gives its $T_{d-1}$ scalar $z_\nu$. Thus $L_d$ acts on this factor by $z_\mu-z_\nu=c(A)-r(A)=i$. The generalized primary projections are exact by [F1]; every occurrence of this factor lies in $E_iD(\mu)$, and none in another summand. Consequently $[E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)]=[D(\mu)\downarrow_{S_{d-1}}:D(\nu)]$, also when both sides are zero. This does not assert that a factor occurs before its multiplicity is computed. [F1, F2, F3, given]

2.1 Apply the local count [F4] to $\lambda=\mu'$ and the ordinary node $A'$. The group dictionary is $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ and likewise for $\nu$; sign restricts to sign, so simultaneous twist preserves the restriction multiplicity. Transposing negates residues and reverses the order of corners in a fixed residue class, as [F5] states. The ordinary piecewise formula is therefore zero when $A$ is not normal, and otherwise is the number of normal $i$-nodes weakly below $A$, counting $A$ itself. Combine this with step 1.1. The unconditioned weakly-below count is not used off normality. [F4, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 For $p=3$ and $\mu=(3,3,2,1,1)$, the normal residue-$2$ nodes are $(3,2)$ and $(5,1)$; the same-residue signature has the two minus signs and no plus sign. The two respective regular removals give multiplicities $2$ and $1$ by step 2.1. At degree one the same argument gives the one-dimensional restriction to $S_0$; degree zero has no removable node. Thus the boundary cases and both displayed cases are included. No Specht-to-restriction Hom criterion is asserted. [F4, F5, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The complete count proof is the local first-level supplier, built from the integral root-interval basis and finite essential-subset recurrence. The cited Kleshchev and Brundan papers document the historical source of this formula; they are not external proof premises. The new local contribution here is the conditional class-sum localization and the exact transpose/sign transport. No unconditional count or implication from a zero form quotient to a zero actual module head is used.

items.title: Conormal-node composition multiplicities under residue induction
items.statement:
In the notation of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]], let
$B$ be an addable $i$-node of the $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ such that
$\nu=\mu\cup B$ is again $p$-restricted, and let $F_i$ be the residue-summand
induction functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $B$ is not a conormal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B':\ B'\ \text{conormal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly above }B\}$$
(counting $B$ itself) if $B$ is conormal. The dual Specht-to-induction Hom
criterion (Kleshchev survey Theorem 11.7(i), Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5 dual
form) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$ of characteristic $p>0$, a $p$-restricted partition $\mu$ of $d$, an addable residue-$i$ node $B$ such that $\nu=\mu+B$ is $p$-restricted, and the actual residue induction functor $F_i$.

[F1] The actual Schur coefficient foundation and root-interval basis/count supplier holds over every field, for arbitrary dominant polynomial weights and all intervals. Negative coefficient words span, positive coefficient words detect, binary-root weight spaces have dimension $E_a(r,s)=\varepsilon_a(r,s)$, and the finite integer recurrence is $E_a(r,s)=\nu_a(r,s)+\sum_{u=r+1}^sE'_a(r,u-1)\nu_a(u,s)$, with $E'_a(r,t)=E_{a+\omega_t}(r,t)$. Its normal-stack proof includes zero coordinates and killed roots ([[lem-type-a-modular-root-interval-essential-subset-basis-and-count]]).

[F2] The proved local $q=1$ Schur/group corner in steps 14.1–15.1 of [[thm-kleshchev-first-level-branching-multiplicity]] identifies the regular Weyl corner and cell form with the Murphy cell and form, with scalar $1$, and proves equality of their radical corners. Thus $L_N(\lambda)e=D(\lambda)$ for restricted $\lambda$ and is zero otherwise; surviving labels are distinct. Its tensorword convention is explicit, and its proof uses ordinary-group survival rather than the held finite-$e$ classifier. The integral ordinary Specht basis and signed-conjugate identification are [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]] and [[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]].

[F3] On the complex ordinary Specht module, the joint Jucys–Murphy spectrum is the tableau-content spectrum ([[thm-jucys-murphy-joint-spectrum-is-the-set-of-tableau-content-vectors]]). Only its integral central operator-identity consequence is used, not any characteristic-zero composition count.

[F4] The boundary signature is read top to bottom with addable $+$, removable $-$ and cancellation $-+$ ([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). The actual primary projections define the direct residue decomposition of induction ([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]). Neither primitive-block classification nor an adjunction transfer of composition counts is used.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $d>0$ take $N=d+1$, pad $\mu$ by zeros, set $a_j=\mu_j-\mu_{j+1}$, let $L=L_N(\mu)$ be the actual Schur simple, $V=F^N$, and $M=V\otimes L$. Tensor coefficient operators are the actual polynomial Schur operators of degree $d+1$, obtained by multiplying the two polynomial matrix actions. This works over finite fields without replacing coefficient actions by evaluated group elements. The case $d=0$ is treated below. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Here is the local component identity used below. If a binary root deficit has separated connected components (a zero simple-root coefficient between consecutive components), its negative words split into products supported on those components. All cross-component positive and negative root operators commute, and their Cartan characters on the other component are unchanged: their simple-root supports are nonadjacent. Move the positive words past the other components and evaluate their highest coefficients one component at a time. The positive/negative coefficient matrix is consequently the tensor product of the component matrices. Negative-word spanning and positive detection identify its quotient by the common positive-test kernel with the actual simple weight space. Hence this weight space is the tensor product of the component quotients, including when one is zero. This proves the assertion directly from coefficient words; it does not assume a tensor-product decomposition of the whole simple module. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct]

3.1 In particular fix one component $\delta$. Choose a negative basis $f_1v,\ldots,f_tv$ of its quotient and positive tests $e_1,\ldots,e_t$ dual to it. They are finite linear combinations of actual coefficient words, with coefficients in $F$; their existence follows from positive detection and ordinary finite-dimensional linear algebra. Then $P_\delta=\sum_{h=1}^t f_he_h$ is the identity on every binary weight space having this component and any separated other components. The same tests apply because the other components change none of the Cartan data of $\delta$. If $t=0$, these weight spaces are zero. This is an identity of coefficient operators on those spaces, so it descends to subquotients. [step 2.1, F1, F2, construct]

4.1 Write $\xi_i=\mu+\epsilon_i$. Suppose a simple composition factor with highest weight $\eta$ contributes at $\xi_i$. All weights of $M$ are at most $\mu+\epsilon_1$, and weights of that factor are at most $\eta$. Thus $\xi_i\le\eta\le\mu+\epsilon_1.$ [step 3.1, F1, F2, construct]

5.1 The deficit $\Gamma=\mu+\epsilon_1-\eta$ has simple-root coefficients $0$ or $1$ in positions $1,\ldots,i-1$ and zero elsewhere. On a tensor summand $v_j\otimes L_{\eta-\epsilon_j}$ the deficit in $L$ is $\Gamma-(\alpha_1+\cdots+\alpha_{j-1}).$ [step 4.1, F1, F2, construct]

6.1 It must be nonnegative. Consequently every possible label $j$ lies before the first missing coefficient in $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma$ has a component $\delta$ after that first gap, every positive or negative coefficient word supported on $\delta$ fixes the $V$ factor (its nonconstant terms annihilate each of these labels). Its action on this tensor weight is therefore purely its action on $L$. The preceding $P_\delta$ is the identity on the entire weight $M_\eta$, not just on individual tensor summands. [step 5.1, F1, F2, construct]

7.1 Choose a composition series and a lift $x\in M_\eta$ of the nonzero highest vector of the proposed factor in its series quotient. Each $e_hx$ lies in the preceding submodule because it has strictly higher weight, and each $f_h$ preserves that submodule. But $P_\delta x=x$ would then place $x$ in it, a contradiction. If the component quotient is zero there was no such tensor weight to start with. Thus $\Gamma$ has no later component. Its only possible nonzero coefficients form one initial interval, and $\eta=\mu+\epsilon_u\quad\text{for some }u\le i.$ [step 6.1, F1, F2, construct]

8.1 This excludes only highest weights of factors contributing to $\xi_i$. It asserts nothing about distant tensor factors. [step 7.1, F1, F2, construct]

9.1 Since every weight of $L$ is at most $\mu$, $M_{\xi_i}=\bigoplus_{j\le i}v_j\otimes L_{\mu+\epsilon_i-\epsilon_j},\qquad d_i:=\dim M_{\xi_i}=1+\sum_{j<i}E_a(j,i-1).$ [step 8.1, F1, F2, construct]

10.1 Let $b_u$ be the actual composition multiplicity of $L_N(\mu+\epsilon_u)$ in $M$ when that weight is dominant; set $b_u=0$ otherwise. No restrictedness condition is imposed on these auxiliary factors. The support lemma and the one-dimensional highest spaces give $d_i=b_i+\sum_{u<i}b_uE_{a+\omega_u}(u,i-1).$ (equation C). [step 9.1, F1, F2, construct]

11.1 Indeed $\mu+\epsilon_u-\xi_i=\alpha_u+\cdots+\alpha_{i-1}$. On this interval the fundamental coordinates of the dominant weight $\mu+\epsilon_u$ are those of $a$ with its first coordinate $u$ increased by one; the coordinate $u-1$ changed by minus one lies outside the interval. Nondominant rows have multiplicity zero, so their formal summands cause no alteration of (C). [step 10.1, F1, F2, construct]

12.1 For completeness the weight-dimension symmetry needed here is local. Permutation matrices permute the integer weight spaces of $L$. Hence its lowest weight is $w_0\mu$, its space is one dimensional, and every weight lies between $w_0\mu$ and $\mu$. The contragredient dual twisted by $\det^d$ is a polynomial simple of highest weight $\mu^*=(d-\mu_N,\ldots,d-\mu_1).$ [step 11.1, F1, F2, construct]

13.1 One can verify polynomiality without a rational-module classification theorem. The tensorword Schur algebra acts faithfully on $V^{\otimes d}$; its regular module embeds in a finite direct sum of copies of this tensor space by its action on a basis. Thus every simple is a subquotient of copies of this tensor space. Duality and the twist make it a subquotient of $(V^*\otimes\det)^{\otimes d}$; the explicit exterior-complement pairing gives $V^*\otimes\det\cong\bigwedge^{N-1}V$ over every field. It is therefore polynomial. Positive and negative coefficients interchange under duality, so the highest weight just identified determines the same actual Schur simple as in the accepted foundation. These statements are coefficient identities; over a finite field they can equivalently be checked over $F(t)$ and descended as the identical finite matrices. [step 12.1, F1, F2, construct]

14.1 Put $\bar a_t=a_{N-t}$. Duality reverses roots and preserves weight dimensions, yielding $E_a(j,i-1)=E_{\bar a}(N-i+1,N-j).$ [step 13.1, F1, F2, construct]

15.1 This argument applies also to any dominant shifted weight. In particular the first-coordinate shift at $u$ becomes the final-coordinate shift at $N-u$ on the reversed interval. No restriction on its fundamental coordinates is needed. [step 14.1, F1, F2, construct]

16.1 Reverse the indices: $r=N-i+1$, $\bar b_r=b_i$, $\bar d_r=d_i$. On indices $1,\ldots,N$, let the strictly upper triangular matrices be $A[r,v]=\nu'_{\bar a}(r,v-1),\qquad B[r,v]=E'_{\bar a}(r,v-1)\quad(r<v).$ [step 15.1, F1, construct]

17.1 For $r<v$, apply the accepted recurrence to $[r,v-1]$ after increasing coordinate $v-1$. Every earlier interval $[r,u-1]$ with $u<v$ is unaffected, while the tail normal count is shifted at $v-1$. Thus $B[r,v]=A[r,v]+\sum_{r<u<v}B[r,u]A[u,v]$, or $B=A+BA$. Hence $(I+B)(I-A)=I$. Since these are finite integer matrices, the inverse is two-sided and $(I+B)^{-1}=I-A$. Equivalently, the supplier's first-cut recurrence gives $B=A+AB$ and $I+B=I+A+\cdots+A^{N-1}$. [step 16.1, F1, construct]

18.1 Let $H_r=\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)$, with $H_N=0$. Applying the accepted recurrence separately for every endpoint and summing gives $\bar d=\mathbf1+(I+B)H.$ [step 17.1, F1, construct]

19.1 Opposition turns (C) into $\bar d=(I+B)\bar b$. Multiplication by $I-A$ gives, as ordinary integers, $b_i=1+\sum_{s=r}^{N-1}\bigl(\nu_{\bar a}(r,s)-\nu'_{\bar a}(r,s)\bigr),\qquad r=N-i+1.$ (equation D). [step 18.1, F1, construct]

20.1 This is finite nilpotent matrix arithmetic. It neither divides in $F$ nor replaces a composition multiplicity by a residue in $F$. [step 19.1, F1, construct]

21.1 Use the accepted normal-stack interpretation; every coordinate and $B,C$ equality tested in this paragraph and the endpoint analysis is modulo $p$, whereas stack heights are ordinary integers. Write $\sigma(r,t)$ for its alive indicator and put $\sigma(r,r-1)=1$. For every dominant coordinate array $\lambda$, $\nu_\lambda(r,s)-\nu'_\lambda(r,s)=\sigma(r,s-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}\right).$ (equation E). [step 20.1, F1, construct]

22.1 If killed before the final step, both counts are zero. Otherwise let its current height be $h\ge1$. The endpoint shift keeps $C(r,s)$ fixed and replaces $B$ and $\lambda_s$ by $B+1$ and $\lambda_s+1$. If $B=-1$ it creates a pop and lowers the count by one; when $\lambda_s=-1$, the unshifted step instead pushes and the shifted zero-coordinate step is neutral, with the same difference. If $B=0$ it removes a pop and increases the count by one; when $\lambda_s=0$, the old step is neutral and the new step pushes, again with that difference. For other $B$ neither change alters the count. If a pop removes the initial root, its new count is zero, still $h-1=0$. At $s=r$ the two counts are $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r\ne0}$ and $\mathbf1_{\lambda_r+1\ne0}$, giving the same formula. These alternatives are exhaustive and valid for $p=2$. [step 21.1, F1, construct]

23.1 Fix an actual addable row $i$ and put $R_j=\mu_j+1-j$, $\rho=R_i\pmod p$. If $i>1$, addability means $a_{i-1}>0$. Since $\mu$ is restricted, $0<a_{i-1}<p$; the reversed root therefore starts alive. For $r=N-i+1$, $s=N-j$, direct substitution gives $B_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_j-R_i-1,\qquad C_{\bar a}(r,s)=R_{j+1}-R_i.$ [step 22.1, F1, F4, construct]

24.1 Thus the two indicators in (E) respectively detect an addable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$ and a removable-position residue $\rho$ in row $j$. The normal stack processes the boundary in reverse order, starting with the chosen $+$ in row $i$. At step $j$ its $C=0$ push corresponds to the plus in row $j+1$, and its $B=0$ pop to the minus in row $j$. The top-row plus is a pending final event. This reversal is exactly the stack evaluation of $-+$ cancellation: in a reverse scan, a minus cancels the most recently encountered plus. [step 23.1, F1, F4, construct]

25.1 Here is the precise check at flat row blocks and at the endpoints. Let $D_s=1+\sum_{t=r}^s\sigma(r,t-1)\left(\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=-1}-\mathbf1_{B(r,t)=0}\right).$ [step 24.1, F1, F4, construct]

26.1 While the chosen root remains alive, $D_s$ is its current normal-stack height plus the pending indicator $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}$, where $j=N-s$. At the initial step the removable event $B(r,r)=0$ cannot occur since $0<a_{i-1}<p$, and this identity follows immediately. At each subsequent live step the change in height is $\mathbf1_{C(r,s)=0}-\mathbf1_{B(r,s)=0}.$ [step 25.1, F1, F4, construct]

27.1 For $a_j\ne0$ these are disjoint push/pop events. For $a_j=0$ the indicators are equal and the step is neutral, as required by the actual stack. Subtracting this height change from the change in $D_s$ gives $\mathbf1_{R_j=R_i}-\mathbf1_{R_{j+1}=R_i},$ [step 26.1, F1, F4, construct]

28.1 which replaces the previous pending indicator by the next. This proves the invariant by induction, including flat blocks. Equivalently, at each flat boundary $a_j=0$, the virtual removable sign in row $j$ and virtual addable sign in row $j+1$ have the same residue and form an adjacent $-+$ pair in the selected-residue row-boundary word. Deleting these pairs restores exactly the actual boundary word. By signature confluence their insertion or deletion has no effect on the surviving actual nodes. The chosen node is an actual addable, so it is never among the virtual pairs. [step 27.1, F1, F4, construct]

29.1 If the initial root is killed, its preceding height was one, the current event is $B=0$, and $B=-1$ is false. The pending indicator after the step is zero. Thus $D_s=0$, and every later term is zero because the alive indicator remains zero. In the reversed boundary scan, killing the initial plus likewise means that the chosen node is canceled; later pluses above it cannot revive it. At the last step the pending indicator is the actual addable top-row plus. We have therefore evaluated exactly the reverse scan of the prefix ending at the chosen node. A minus below this prefix cannot cancel a plus in it under top-to-bottom $-+$ cancellation; the conormal decisions for this prefix agree with those in the entire signature. [step 28.1, F1, F4, construct]

30.1 Consequently (D) is zero precisely when the chosen plus is canceled. If it survives, (D) is the number of surviving pluses of residue $\rho$ in the prefix, namely the number of conormal nodes weakly above $B$. For $i=1$, (D) is $b_1=1$: the top plus survives and it is the only node weakly above itself. For completeness, a nondominant row $i>1$ has $a_{i-1}=0$; the first endpoint difference is $-1$, killing the virtual initial unit and all later differences, so (D) gives zero as required by (C). These rows were not silently discarded during the integer inversion. [step 29.1, F1, F4, construct]

31.1 Let $\omega=(1^N)$ be the regular degree-$N$ weight. Then $M_\omega=\bigoplus_{j=1}^N v_j\otimes L_{\omega-\epsilon_j}.$ [step 30.1, F2, construct]

32.1 Let $G=\mathfrak S_N$, $H=\mathfrak S_d$ fixing label $N$, and $W=L_{\omega-\epsilon_N}$. The accepted local $q=1$ corner/form calculation applies to degree $d$ and rank $N$ with regular weight $(1^d,0)$: its surviving semistandard indices are precisely standard tableaux, and evaluating the corner at $1$ gives the same Murphy basis and scalar-$1$ form, regardless of the unused last label. Its radical-corner equality therefore makes $W$ the left group module $D(\mu)$. To fix the action convention, the supplier's right corner element $\rho_h$ permutes tensorword labels by $h^{-1}$; star conversion makes left $g$ act by right $g^{-1}$, hence by label permutation $g$. The same conversion in the degree-$N$ corner gives the output action. Thus the output regular-corner action is ordinary permutation of labels: on tensorwords the corresponding orbit matrix is exactly that label permutation. Since these are identities in the actual tensorword Schur algebra, the same equality holds on $M$; it does not depend on evaluated permutation matrices spanning the Schur algebra. [step 31.1, F2, construct]

33.1 The explicit map $F[G]\otimes_{F[H]}W\longrightarrow M_\omega,\qquad g\otimes w\longmapsto g(v_N\otimes w)$. [step 32.1, F2, construct]

34.1 is well defined and $G$-equivariant. Left cosets of $H$ correspond to the image label $gN$, and their summands map bijectively to the displayed summands of $M_\omega$. It is therefore an isomorphism. This proves $M_\omega\cong\operatorname{Ind}_{\mathfrak S_d}^{\mathfrak S_{d+1}}D(\mu)$, without Frobenius reciprocity or an adjunction multiplicity assertion. [step 33.1, F2, construct]

35.1 Corner projection is exact. Each Schur composition factor $L_N(\eta)$ projects to the distinct restricted group simple $D(\eta)$ if $\eta$ is restricted, and to zero otherwise, by the accepted local form/radical and ordinary-group survival proof. Hence for a restricted $\mu+B=\mu+\epsilon_i$, its total induction multiplicity is exactly $b_i$. Nonrestricted near factors were kept until this exact projection. Distant factors were never excluded; distinct surviving labels ensure that they cannot change this particular count. When $d=0$, the single degree-one tensor/corner gives the unique plus and multiplicity one directly. [step 34.1, F2, construct]

36.1 The generalized Jucys--Murphy induction summands give a direct decomposition of total induction. For the ordinary group elements $L_k=\sum_{j<k}(j,k)$, induction by inserting the letter $n$ into a cycle gives the integral identity $\prod_{k=1}^n(t+L_k)=\sum_{g\in\mathfrak S_n}t^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g.$ [step 35.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

37.1 The factor $t$ makes $n$ a new fixed point; each transposition $(j,n)$ inserts $n$ at the uniquely specified place in the cycle containing $j$. These alternatives are disjoint and exhaust the permutations. Coefficients on the right are class sums, so all coefficients of $Q_n(t)=\prod_{k=1}^n(t-L_k)$ are central over the integers and every field. [step 36.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

38.1 The published [[thm-jucys-murphy-joint-spectrum-is-the-set-of-tableau-content-vectors]] says that $Q_n(t)$ acts on the complex ordinary Specht module of shape $\lambda$ as $\prod_{A\in\lambda}(t-\operatorname{res}_{\mathbb Z}(A))$. The ordinary integral Specht lattice has the free polytabloid basis provided by the accepted integral bridge. The operator equality has integer matrices on that lattice; its validity after scalar extension to $\mathbb C$ therefore implies its validity over $\mathbb Z$. Reducing and taking its radical quotient proves the same content scalar on ordinary $D^\lambda$ over every field. The accepted signed-conjugate dictionary sends each $L_k$ to $-L_k$ under the sign twist, and transpose negates contents. Hence $Q_n(t)$ acts on restricted $D(\lambda)=D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ by the content polynomial of $\lambda$. This use of the published complex spectrum is an integral operator-identity descent; none of the multiplicity inversion uses characteristic-zero composition counts or semisimplicity. [step 37.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

39.1 Let $\alpha$ be the multiset of residues of $\mu$. The exact central content polynomial on $D(\mu)$ and the central CRT description of the content sums give $e_\alpha^{(d)}D(\mu)=D(\mu)$; this requires no primitive-block assertion. For clarity the functor idempotent $e=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,h}$ implies the following test on $F_hD(\mu)=F\mathfrak S_{d+1}e\otimes_{F\mathfrak S_d}D(\mu)$. On its generating subspace $e\otimes D(\mu)$, the first-$d$ content polynomial has exactly the scalar for $\mu$, and $L_{d+1}-h$ is nilpotent. These operators commute and $(L_{d+1}-h)^m e=0$ for a fixed primary exponent $m$. A coefficient $z$ of $Q_{d+1}(t)-(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$ is central by the integral identity. On $e\otimes w$ it is the corresponding scalar coefficient of $Q_\mu(t)$ times $h-L_{d+1}$: balance the first-$d$ central coefficient across $e$ into $w$. Centrality lets this same calculation iterate, so $z^m(e\otimes w)=0$. Since the whole module is generated by these vectors and $z$ commutes with every group translate, $z^m$ is zero on the whole module. On a simple factor a nilpotent central endomorphism is zero, since every nonzero simple-module endomorphism is invertible. Thus every factor in this summand has content polynomial $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)$. [step 38.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

40.1 Distinct residues give distinct polynomials: $(t-h)Q_\mu(t)-(t-k)Q_\mu(t)=(k-h)Q_\mu(t)\ne0$ for $h\ne k$. The content polynomial of $\mu+B$ appends exactly the residue of $B$. Its factors therefore occur only in the corresponding residue summand. The total multiplicity computed above is exactly the multiplicity in $F_iD(\mu)$ required by the target. This argument does not use primitivity or exhaustiveness of any content-block idempotent. [step 39.1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

41.1 Transpose preserves boundary types. Literally $(\mu\cup B)'=\mu'\cup B^{\mathsf t},\qquad(\mu\setminus A)'=\mu'\setminus A^{\mathsf t}.$ [step 40.1, F4, construct]

42.1 It sends an addable node to an addable node and a removable node to a removable node; it negates the residue. The appropriate boundary reading order is reversed when transporting the signature convention. It does not exchange addable and removable sets. The proof above needs no claimed equality of induction and restriction multiplicities and no transpose transfer of a restriction count. [step 41.1, F4, construct]

43.1 The finite character inversion, boundary-stack calculation, exact induction corner and residue allocation just proved identify the stated multiplicity with zero off conormality and with the conormal weak-above count on conormality. Both cases hold over every field of characteristic $p$, with nonrestricted auxiliary factors retained until projection and no assertion about other tensor factors. [step 42.1, F1, F2, F4, construct] ∎

## Remarks

The survey documents the formula's origin; its count is not a proof premise. Biadjunction does not equate these composition multiplicities: in characteristic $2$, induction of $D(1)$ to $S_2$ has multiplicity $2$ of $D(1,1)$, whereas restricting that simple has multiplicity $1$ of $D(1)$. The proof instead uses actual tensor weights, finite integer inversion and an explicit coset map.

items.title: The good node gives the simple socle and head of the residue restriction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$; let $A$ be the good
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). For the
residue-summand functor $E_i$ of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]] the
module $E_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to
$D(\nu)$, and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(\nu)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$ is
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. Thus the Loewy endpoints are simple even though the
formal character of $E_iD(\mu)$ may contain the additional normal-node
factors of
[[thm-normal-node-composition-multiplicities-under-residue-restriction]].
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Socle. By [F5] the socle of $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)= igoplus_jE_jD(\mu)$ is $ igoplus_j\operatorname{soc}(E_jD(\mu))$. By [F1] the socle of the restriction is the multiplicity-free sum of the $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ over the good nodes, and by [F2] each summand $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ lies in $E_jD(\mu)$ with its residue $j$; since a nonzero submodule of $E_jD(\mu)$ cannot lie in $ igoplus_{l
e j}E_lD(\mu)$ by the directness of the sum, the $j$-summand of the socle is exactly the single simple module $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ and $\operatorname{soc}(E_jD(\mu))=D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ is simple. For $j=i$ this gives $\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))=D(\mu\setminus A)=D(
u)$. [given, F1, F2, F5]

2.1 Multiplicity. Applying the normal-node theorem [F3] with $X=A$: since $A$ is a normal $i$-node, $[E_iD(\mu):D(
u)]$ is the number of normal $i$-nodes of $\mu$ weakly below $A$ counting $A$; by [F6] this is $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$. [step 1.1, F3, F6]

2.2 Head. By [F4] the module $E_iD(\mu)$ is self-dual; by [F5] its head is the dual of its socle, $\operatorname{hd}(E_iD(\mu))\cong(\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu)))^*$, which by step 1.1 is $D(
u)^*\cong D(
u)$ because $D(
u)$ is self-dual by [F4]. Hence the head is simple and isomorphic to $D(
u)$. [step 1.1, F4, F5]

3.1 Conclusion. Step 1.1 gives simple socle $D(
u)$, step 2.1 the total multiplicity $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ of $D(
u)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$, and step 2.2 simple head $D(
u)$. The additional normal-node composition factors of [F3] may occur in the middle Loewy layers; the statement asserts only the endpoints and the total multiplicity, and no graded shift is displayed before the Hecke/KLR bridge. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

references.title: Alexander Kleshchev, Representation Theory of Symmetric Groups and Related Hecke Algebras, Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 47 (2010) 419-481, author arXiv version; §11.4 with Theorem 11.6(ii) and the socle statement, printed pp. 53-54, and Theorem 7.4 with §11.3 for the epsilon_i-multiplicity. Complete 66-page text, SHA-256 8685199608967fa7c479e4dd883990b716a6f708e71cf75f6ce4aba41c6f2cab

Jonathan Brundan, Modular Branching Rules and the Mullineux Map for Hecke Algebras of Type A, Proc. London Math. Soc. (3) 77 (1998) 551-581; complete 34-page author manuscript, Theorems 2.6 and 5.4 with §5.5-5.7, printed pp. 4-5 and 28-32 (the proof-bearing treatment of the good-node socle in the Hecke convention)

items.title: The cogood node gives the simple socle and head of the residue induction
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varphi_i(\mu)>0$; let $B$ be the cogood
$i$-node and $\nu=\mu\cup B$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$F_iD(\mu)$ has simple socle and simple head, both isomorphic to $D(\nu)$,
and the total (ungraded) multiplicity of $D(\nu)$ in $F_iD(\mu)$ is
$\varphi_i(\mu)$
([[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]).
items.strategy:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 We first establish the restriction endpoint locally. Work with left Schur modules through star. In tensor degree $m$, the word of $m_\alpha T_w$ has $j$th letter the row containing $j$ in $t^\alpha w$; at regular type it is $jw^{-1}$, with zero-multiplicity labels omitted. Over $K=F(t)$ the evaluations $g^{\otimes m}$ span the tensor Schur algebra: a functional killing them gives a polynomial zero on invertible matrices; multiplication by $\det$ and the infinite-field polynomial identity force that polynomial to be zero. Schur simples are therefore simple polynomial $\mathrm{GL}_N$ modules. The canonical shape/type diagonal is its permutation-summand projection, whose square gives canonical form value one. Semistandard column strictness bounds entries at most $k$ by the first $k$ rows, so all weights are dominated by the highest weight $\xi$ and the highest space is $Kv$. Integer torus characters, rather than Lie eigenvalues modulo $p$, distinguish these weights. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 Gaussian factorization $g=u^-tu^+$ on the big cell shows that negative coefficient operators on $v$ span its simple module: a functional killing them kills $gv$ on that open set and hence everywhere by polynomial identity. Similarly, positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\xi-\Gamma$. If every positive highest coefficient vanished, the highest coefficient of $gx$ would vanish on the big cell, because negative operators cannot raise any weight to $\xi$; it would then vanish on the orbit of $x$, which spans the simple and contains $v$. All coefficient operators have integral tensor replacement matrices, and the ranks and Hom kernels of finite matrices preserve extension from $F$ to $K$. These arguments consequently descend to $F$. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Let $\xi_N=0$, $l=N-1$, and let $M$ be the full last-coordinate-one subspace of $L_N(\xi)$. A primitive vector means one killed by every nonconstant coefficient of the upper Levi unipotent group, not merely by its Lie generators. Factor the full upper group as $V U_l^+$, where $V$ has only the last column above the diagonal nontrivial. A positive test of a Levi-primitive vector acts only through $V$, since the right-hand nonconstant Levi coefficients kill it. Raising last coordinate $1$ to highest coordinate $0$ requires a $V$ monomial of degree exactly one. Positive detection therefore gives $E_{rN}x=cv\ne0$ for some $r$. Hence $\operatorname{wt}(x)=\xi-\beta_r$, where $\beta_r=\alpha_r+\cdots+\alpha_l$, even when the initial first-level deficit was arbitrary. On that primitive weight space $x\mapsto E_{rN}x$ is injective by the same detection argument, so its dimension is at most one. [step 2.1, construct]

4.1 Put $a_j=\xi_j-\xi_{j+1}$ and use $B(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^s a_j$ and $C(r,s)=s-r+\sum_{j=r}^{s-1}a_j$. For nonempty $I$, the canonical $Q(I)$ kills a primitive vector: if $b=\min I$, its ascending-prefix letter $e_{b-1}$ commutes past the remaining ascending letters, whose indices exceed $b$, and becomes a rightmost Levi letter with $b-1<l$. Expand a nonzero primitive vector of weight $\xi-\beta_r$ in the essential $T$ basis and select the largest hat among its nonzero coefficients. The triangular pivot isolates a nonzero term. That hat cannot be nonempty, since its $Q$ test would annihilate the vector. Distinct essential hats therefore leave exactly one essential set with empty hat. Empty is linked precisely to a regular set, and the essential-regular matching theorem says such a set exists precisely when $r$ is normal. This proves necessity of normality. [step 3.1, F2, construct]

5.1 Conversely, for normal $r$ let $R_r=\{s\in(r,l]:B(r,s)=0\}$ and choose its compensation $f$ with $r<f(s)\le s$ and $B(f(s),s)=0$. Put $D=f(R_r)$. The inverse matching makes $D$ regular, so its hat is empty. The matched norm is $\Xi_{r,l}(D)=\prod_{s\in[r,l]\setminus R_r}B(r,s)\ne0$: $B(r,r)=a_r\ne0$, and $R_r$ removes exactly the other zero factors. Thus $T_{r,l}(D)v$ is nonzero, and the maximal-hat assertion gives $h(I,D)=0$ for every nonempty $I$. For $r\le j<l$, every positive test of $e_jT(D)v$ has grade $\beta_r-\alpha_j$. Expanding its root matrices into simple words and appending the rightmost $e_j$ gives full words with nonempty canonical $Q$ index, since $e_j$ acts before $e_{j+1}$. All highest coefficients vanish, so positive detection gives $e_jT(D)v=0$. For $j<r$ the target weight is outside dominance below $\xi$ and is zero. A nonconstant Levi coefficient whose weight is not bounded by $\beta_r$ likewise has zero target. At a weight bounded by $\beta_r$, root-variable exponents are at most one, so the coefficient is a product of positive root matrices, each an iterated simple-root commutator; its rightmost root kills the vector. This proves full group primitivity. The primitive line at $\xi-\beta_r$ is consequently one-dimensional exactly at normal $r$, and we denote any nonzero vector on it by $v_r$. [step 4.1, F2, construct]

6.1 We separate primitive labels integrally, including $p=2$. In tensor degree $b$ for Levi rank $l$, put $H_a=E_{aa}$ and define $\binom{H_a}{2}$ to act on a weight $\zeta$ by the integer $\binom{\zeta_a}{2}$ reduced in $F$. Concretely it is $\sum_{x<y}E_{aa}^{(x)}E_{aa}^{(y)}$, with no division by $2$ in $F$. The tensor action $Z_b$ of the group central transposition sum $z_b=\sum_{x<y}(x,y)$ satisfies the exact integer identity $Z_b=\sum_a\binom{H_a}{2}+\sum_{a<c}(E_{ac}E_{ca}-H_a)$. The equal-position part of $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ is $H_a$; after subtracting it, the terms are exactly the two swaps of unequal labels. The diagonal terms count equal-label pairs. Since $z_b$ commutes with the position group and every Schur endomorphism, this operator belongs to the Schur algebra and is central. [step 5.1, construct]

7.1 On a primitive vector of dominant weight $\zeta$, $E_{ac}$ kills it for $a<c$, so $E_{ac}E_{ca}$ acts by $H_a-H_c$. Therefore $Z_b$ has scalar $\kappa(\zeta)=\sum_a\binom{\zeta_a}{2}-\sum_c(c-1)\zeta_c=\sum_{(c,j)\in[\zeta]}(j-c)$. The binomial here is the actual diagonal weight operator of step 6.1. Centrality makes this scalar constant on the cyclic module generated by the vector. For first-level $\zeta_r=(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_l)-\epsilon_r$, it is $\kappa(\zeta_r)=\kappa(\xi)- (\xi_r-r)$, so $\kappa(\zeta_t)-\kappa(\zeta_r)=-C(t,r)$. Thus the cyclic Levi module $\Psi_r$ generated by $v_r$ cannot contain another primitive $v_t$ when $C(t,r)\ne0$. Equality of the scalars alone does not prove simplicity; we treat it explicitly next. [step 6.1, construct]

8.1 Suppose $t<r$ are normal and $C(t,r)=0$. Choose $D$ for the demands of $r$ as in step 5.1. For $w\ge r$, $B(t,w)=B(r,w)$, and $B(t,r)=a_r\ne0$. The demands of $t$ split into $Y=\{y\in(t,r):B(t,y)=0\}$ and $R_r$. Compensation for $Y$, inherited from normality of $t$, has image $E$ below $r$. Since $B(t,r-1)=C(t,r)-1=-1\ne0$, all those targets and $E$ lie at most $r-2$. Combining their matching with $D$ gives compensation for every demand of $t$, so choose $v_t=T_{t,l}(E\cup D)v$ and $v_r=T_{r,l}(D)v$. For each $e\in E$ its matched $y$ gives $B(e,y)=B(t,y)=0$, hence $C(t,e)=0$. If $E\ne\varnothing$ and $e=\max E$, then $C(e,r)=C(t,r)-C(t,e)=0$. [step 7.1, construct]

9.1 Splitting (P) gives $T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r=v_t-T_{t,l}((E\setminus\{e\})\cup\{r\}\cup D)v-C(e,r)T_{t,l}(E\cup\{r\}\cup D)v$. The last term is zero. The middle term has a (Z) witness with endpoint $r-1$, outside its cuts because $E\le r-2$ and $D>r$. Removing matched source $e$ releases its zero-$B$ target $y_e$; assign $t$ to $y_e$ and retain the matching on $E\setminus\{e\}$. All distinct bounded targets are below $r-1$. Hence that term is zero as well. For $E=\varnothing$, (P) omits the middle term and its last coefficient is $C(t,r)=0$. In both cases $v_t=T_{t,r-1}(E)v_r\in\Psi_r$, without a field denominator. [step 8.1, F2, construct]

10.1 The Gaussian argument on a cyclic module, without assuming simplicity, shows that $\Psi_r$ is spanned by negative Levi coefficients on $v_r$ and has weights at most $\zeta_r$. Any nonzero proper Schur submodule contains a simple Schur submodule and thus a primitive $v_t$ by step 3.1. Dominance gives $t\le r$. For $t=r$, its one-dimensional line is the generating line and would generate all of $\Psi_r$; thus a proper submodule has $t<r$, and the central scalar requires $C(t,r)=0$. Conversely, such an earlier normal $t$ gives a proper nonzero $\Psi_t\subset\Psi_r$ by step 9.1, since its weights are at most $\zeta_t<\zeta_r$. Consequently $\Psi_r$ is simple precisely when $r$ is normal with no earlier normal $t$ satisfying $C(t,r)=0$. All simple Schur submodules of $M$ are exactly these $\Psi_r$, each once: every simple has a primitive highest vector, and each primitive line has dimension one. [step 9.1, F1, construct]

11.1 Now assume $\xi$ restricted. The root criterion is its physical signature criterion: $a_r\ne0$ identifies the removable node in row $r$; scanning $j>r$, a nonzero $a_j$ gives a removable push if $C(r,j)=0$ and an addable pop at row $j+1$ if $B(r,j)=0$. These events have the residue of row $r$; at $a_j=0$ the matching slot supplies and consumes itself and is neutral. For $0<a_j<p$, the two events are disjoint. The compensation-prefix inequalities are exactly survival of the initial push in the signature stack. Also $C(t,r)=(\xi_t-t)-(\xi_r-r)$ compares the residues. Thus the simple cyclic modules in step 10.1 are exactly at the good nodes. Their lower labels are restricted: removing row $r$ decreases $a_r$ by one and increases $a_{r-1}$ by one. The only failure, when $r>1$, would be $a_{r-1}=p-1$. Then $C(r-1,r)=0$, and $r-1$ is also normal, since its later demands are those of $r$, $B(r-1,r)=a_r\ne0$, and the compensation for $r$ is also valid for $r-1$. This contradicts goodness. Hence every Schur socle factor survives the restricted-label corner; no assertion is made about the other composition factors. [step 10.1, F5, construct]

12.1 To transfer without a held generic classifier, for $\xi\vdash m$ choose $N=m+1$ and the regular composition $\omega=(1^{m-1},0,1)$, so $\xi_N=0$ even for columns. Compute the cell corner temporarily in its original right-module convention, then transport through star. Its permutation summand is $M^\omega=FS_m$, and its actual projection $e$ gives $eSe=FS_m$ via $\rho_h(x)=hx$. Type-$\omega$ tableaux correspond to standard tableaux by increasing relabeling $1,\ldots,m-1,N$ to $1,\ldots,m$. Their normalized map fibers are singleton, and evaluation at $1$ sends $\varphi_{st}$ to $m_{st}$. Higher ideals correspond as equality of corner basis spans. The Weyl weight projection keeps exactly these basis vectors; read its cell action using a fixed outer index of the same type and evaluate at $1$ to get the Murphy action. Thus $W^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)$ with the actual same-shape normalization. [step 11.1, F1, F3, construct]

13.1 In the Schur cell product choose all four indices $a,s,t,b$ standard of type $\omega$. Evaluation at $1$ turns $\varphi_{as}\varphi_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)\varphi_{ab}$ into $m_{as}m_{tb}\equiv B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)m_{ab}$, so the unique Murphy coefficient gives $B_\zeta(w_s,w_t)=G_\zeta(c_s,c_t)$. The factor is one. Since $e^*=e$, the Weyl splitting $W=We\oplus W(1-e)$ is orthogonal, giving $\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(We)=\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}(W)e$, including zero corner forms. Projection is exact by lifting $ye$ through $xe$ and taking kernels fixed by $e$. Hence $L^\zeta e\cong C_M(\zeta)/\operatorname{rad}_{\rm form}$. The actual $q=1$ form-unit bridge identifies it with $D^{\zeta'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, nonzero exactly when $\zeta'$ is regular. Transporting these right-cell identities through star gives the corresponding left corners $eW^\zeta$ and $eL^\zeta$ used below. Their nonzero images are exactly the distinct absolutely simple restricted-label modules $D(\zeta)$, with the inverse group convention fixed by the nondegenerate quotient form. [step 12.1, F3, construct]

14.1 Let $\pi_1$ be the sum of actual weight projections with last coordinate one, so $M=\pi_1L_N(\xi)$. The lower Schur orbit matrix $E_A$ embeds as $E_{\operatorname{diag}(A,1)}$; on each word with one $N$ it preserves that position and applies $E_A$ to the remaining ordered positions. Products agree and the lower identity is $\pi_1$, and transpose/star is respected. The lower regular projection of $\omega'=(1^{m-1},0)$ maps to $e$. On the coset-word convention of step 1.1, $\rho'_h$ acts by label permutation $h^{-1}$ on the used lower labels, fixing $N$, identically to $\rho_h$ for the subgroup fixing the last entry of $S_m$. Thus, in the left convention, $e'M=eL_N(\xi)\downarrow_{S_{m-1}}$. Write $S_L=S(N-1,m-1)$ for this lower Schur algebra; every socle and corner lift of $M$ below is over $S_L$. The inverse/star equivalence passes between right and left modules and commutes with this embedding, restriction and sign; the ordinary simple labels are fixed by their nondegenerate invariant quotient forms. No self-duality of a degenerate Specht module is assumed. [step 13.1, construct]

15.1 Socle preservation requires more than exactness. By step 11.1 every Schur socle simple of $M$ survives $e'$. A nonzero Schur submodule killed by $e'$ would contain a simple submodule inside that socle, whose corner is nonzero, a contradiction. Now a group-simple injection $j:D\to e'M$ corresponds to $S_Le'\otimes_{e'S_Le'}D\to M$, $se'\otimes x\mapsto sj(x)$, $s\in S_L$. Its image $I$ is generated by its corner $e'I=j(D)$. A proper Schur submodule $J$ of $I$ has either $e'J=0$, excluded by the no-killed-submodule property, or $e'J=e'I$, which generates $I$ and forces $J=I$. Thus $I$ is simple. Every group-simple corner submodule lifts to an actual Schur simple submodule, and conversely every surviving Schur simple has simple corner. Exactness on the semisimple sum, distinct labels and the one-dimensional primitive lines yield $\operatorname{soc}_{FS_{m-1}}(e'M)=e'\operatorname{soc}_{S_L} M$, multiplicity-free with exactly the good-deletion labels. The unused coordinate includes columns and $m=1$, whose lower degree-zero corner is $F$. [step 14.1, F1, construct]

16.1 The group central $z_m$ acts on $D(\xi)$ by $\kappa(\xi)$, since its tensor action is step 6.1 and its regular-summand action is $\rho_{z_m}$; right multiplication equals left multiplication for this central element. On the good lower label it acts by $\kappa(\xi-A)$. Therefore $L_m=z_m-z_{m-1}$ has scalar $\operatorname{res}(A)$ on that simple submodule, with the restricted convention $c-r$. Primary projection selects just that residue, and socles respect the actual direct sum. We obtain $\operatorname{soc}E_iD(\xi)=D(\xi-A_i)$ when $\varepsilon_i(\xi)>0$, and zero otherwise. In the latter case $E_iD(\xi)=0$, since a nonzero finite-dimensional module contains a simple submodule. [step 15.1, F5, construct]

17.1 The invariant nondegenerate quotient form makes $D(\xi)$ self-dual. A primary polynomial projector in $L_m$ is self-adjoint, since the inverse involution fixes $L_m$, so its summand has a restricted nondegenerate invariant form. Its head is therefore dual to its simple socle and is the same simple. Thus for every restricted $\eta,\tau$ of consecutive degrees, $\dim_F\operatorname{Hom}(E_iD(\eta),D(\tau))$ is one if $\varepsilon_i(\eta)>0$ and $\eta-\operatorname{good}_i(\eta)=\tau$, and zero otherwise. The scalar endomorphism ring is $F$ by absolute simplicity. This all-pairs criterion includes the zero case and all initially possible primitive weights; it does not discard middle composition factors. [step 16.1, F3, F5, construct]

18.1 We justify the needed functor interfaces locally. In $\mathbb ZS_n$ the Jucys identity is $\prod_{r=1}^n(u+L_r)=\sum_{g\in S_n}u^{\#\operatorname{cycles}(g)}g$. Induct on $n$: choosing $u$ leaves $n$ fixed, and choosing $(a,n)$ inserts it next to $a$ in a cycle, bijectively covering the non-fixed permutations. Hence each elementary symmetric JM coefficient is central over every field. On a simultaneous primary tuple these operators have generalized eigenvalues equal to its elementary symmetric residue coefficients; nilpotence follows by expanding a polynomial in the commuting nilpotent differences. Distinct residue multisets have distinct coefficient tuples, since their monic products of prime-field linear factors retain multiplicities uniquely even in characteristic $p$. For each elementary symmetric operator, construct its univariate primary projectors by the same polynomial CRT construction as in [F5], then multiply these commuting projectors. This gives the content projector equal to the sum of tuple projectors of that content. This proves content centrality without factorial division, position-dependent symmetric-polynomial claims, or content-block primitivity. The projectors are inverse-fixed. For an input in content $\alpha$, induction projection by right $e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$ is the same as right $P_{d+1,i}$, because $ge_\alpha\otimes x=g\otimes e_\alpha x$. An absolutely simple $D(\mu)$ lies in exactly one of these central contents, since their scalar idempotents are orthogonal and sum to one; denote it by $\alpha$. Thus these interfaces agree with the actual functor definition. [step 17.1, F5, construct]

19.1 Put $G=S_{d+1}$, $H=S_d$, and let $E_H:FG\to FH$ truncate group coefficients. For left modules the natural Frobenius map is $\Phi(g\otimes x)(y)=E_H(yg)x$, with coinduction action $(a q)(y)=q(ya)$. It is balanced and $G$-linear by $E_H(hz)=hE_H(z)$ and $E_H(zh)=E_H(z)h$. For a left-coset transversal $T$ of $G/H$, its inverse is $\Psi(q)=\sum_{r\in T}r\otimes q(r^{-1})$. The right cosets $Hr^{-1}$ partition $G$, so evaluation at $y$ has exactly the term $yr\in H$ and returns $q(y)$. On $g\otimes x$ the unique term with $r^{-1}g\in H$ balances back to $g\otimes x$. These verify both identities and naturality with correct cosets and only finite choices. [step 18.1, construct]

20.1 Let $e=e_\alpha P_{d+1,i}$, commuting with $FH$ and inverse-fixed. For any such centralizer element, $E_H(eZ)=E_H(Ze)$: the coefficient at $h$ is the group coefficient trace $\tau(h^{-1}eZ)=\tau(h^{-1}Ze)$, by cyclicity and commuting $e$ with $h^{-1}$. Under $\Phi$, the value at one of right projection $R_e$ is consequently $q(e)$. If $f:N\to\operatorname{Coind}X$ is $G$-linear, $f(en)(1)=f(n)(e)$. Evaluation therefore identifies projected maps $N\to F_iX$ with $H$-maps $E_iN\to X$; conversely an $H$-map extends via $q_n(y)=h(eyn)$, with $h:E_iN\to X$ evaluated after the projector $e$. For $X=e_\alpha X$, every $H$-map already selects the matching content. Thus $\operatorname{Hom}_G(N,F_iX)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_H(E_iN,X)$ exactly, with no duality shift and no asserted equality of composition multiplicities. [step 19.1, construct]

21.1 The labelled signature inverse is local. Adding or removing a corner flips its $i$-sign, and the other boundary statuses that can change have residues $i\pm1$, not $i$ for $p\ge2$. In the stack reduction, flipping the last surviving plus gives the first surviving minus and conversely: before that position the minus stack is empty, and its distinguished minus survives exactly when every suffix prefix has at least as many minus pushes as plus pops, equivalent to no later plus surviving after the flip. Good removal preserves restrictedness by step 11.1. Cogood addition also does: its only possible new forbidden difference is $a_r=p-1$, in which case the addable node in row $r+1$ has the same residue, with no $i$-node between the two pluses. If the earlier plus survives, the later one also survives, contradicting that the earlier is cogood. Hence addition remains restricted and the inverse holds in both directions. In particular $B$ is cogood for $\mu$ exactly when it is good for $\nu=\mu\cup B$. No equality between $\varepsilon_i(\nu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ is used. [step 20.1, F5, construct]

22.1 Apply step 20.1 with $N=D(\eta)$ and $X=D(\mu)$ for every restricted $\eta\vdash d+1$. By step 17.1 the resulting Hom space is one-dimensional precisely when $\eta-\operatorname{good}_i(\eta)=\mu$, and zero otherwise. Step 21.1 makes exactly one such label, namely $\nu=\mu\cup B$. The group simple classification covers every simple by these absolutely irreducible labels. The dimensions of all simple-to-module Hom spaces therefore identify the socle of $F_iD(\mu)$ as the single $D(\nu)$, with socle multiplicity one, excluding every other label. [step 21.1, F3, construct]

23.1 Give $\operatorname{Ind}_H^G D(\mu)$ the invariant nondegenerate coset form $\beta(r\otimes x,s\otimes y)=\delta_{rs}\beta_\mu(x,y)$ on a finite left transversal. A group element permutes cosets and acts by $H$ on the fibers, proving invariance. Equivalently its value on general group representatives is $\beta_\mu(x,E_H(g^{-1}h)y)$. The projection $R_e$ is self-adjoint: moving it to the first argument gives $E_H(e^*g^{-1}h)$, which equals $E_H(g^{-1}he^*)$ by the trace calculation of step 20.1, and $e^*=e$. Its image is orthogonal to the complement and inherits a nondegenerate invariant form. Thus $F_iD(\mu)$ is self-dual, and its head is the dual of its simple socle, namely $D(\nu)$ through the nondegenerate invariant quotient form. This proves both endpoints, including characteristic two. [step 22.1, F3, F5, construct]

24.1 For $d=0$, the empty partition has one conormal node $(1,1)$ of residue zero and $\varphi_0=1$. Induction from $S_0$ to $S_1$ is $F$, with $L_1=0$, so $F_0D(\varnothing)=D(1)=F$ has these endpoints; other residue functors are zero. Every use of $F(t)$ above descends to the original field: weight projections and coefficient operators have matrices over $F$, finite Hom ranks preserve extension, and the simple Schur and group labels remain absolutely simple. Therefore the endpoint assertions hold over every original field of characteristic $p$. [step 23.1, F1, F3, construct]

25.1 The total multiplicity is the separate use of [F4]. Apply it to the cogood $B$, which is bottommost conormal. Its conormal nodes weakly above it are exactly all $\varphi_i(\mu)$ conormal nodes, so $[F_iD(\mu):D(\nu)]=\varphi_i(\mu)$. Combining this count with the independently constructed endpoints proves the full statement. The implication uses no equality of induction and restriction composition counts and no equality $\varepsilon_i(\nu)=\varphi_i(\mu)$. [step 24.1, F4, F5, construct] ∎

items.title: The Schur functor compares first-level branching with Hecke restriction
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field, $q\in F^\times$, $\ell=e(F,q)$, and $n\ge r\ge1$; at the empty lower-rank boundary put $S(0,0)=H(0)=F$ with its identity functor. Use the left-module version of the q-Schur algebra $S(n,r)$ and its exact Schur functor $f_{n,r}:V\mapsto eV$ with left adjoint $h_{n,r}:X\mapsto S(n,r)e\otimes_{eS(n,r)e}X$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]). Right-module suppliers are converted to left modules through their star anti-involutions. All Specht and simple labels below are **Murphy labels**: $f(W^\mu)=S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $f(L_n(\mu))=D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, the latter nonzero exactly when $\mu$ is $\ell$-restricted ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

For a degree-$r$ polynomial module $V=\bigoplus_{|\alpha|=r}V_\alpha$, its **first level** is $$V^1:=\bigoplus_{\alpha_n=1}V_\alpha.$$ It is a module for the Levi polynomial algebra $S(n-1,r-1)$: the first $n-1$ coordinates sum to $r-1$. It is not the sum of the weights one simple root below the highest weight. For an $\ell$-restricted partition $\lambda\vdash r$, the following hold.

1. There is a natural $H(r-1)$-module isomorphism $$f_{n-1,r-1}(L_n(\lambda)^1)\cong      \operatorname{Res}_{H(r-1)}^{H(r)}f_{n,r}(L_n(\lambda)).$$ 2. For any $S(n,r)$-modules $W,V$ with $W^{(e)}=W$ and $V_{(e)}=0$, the Schur functor induces $$\operatorname{Hom}_{S(n,r)}(W,V)\cong      \operatorname{Hom}_{H(r)}(fW,fV).$$ Here $W^{(e)}=S(n,r)eW$ is the intersection of submodules whose quotient is killed by $e$, and $V_{(e)}$ is the sum of submodules killed by $e$. 3. The socle of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ as a Levi module has only $\ell$-restricted labels.

For every partition $\mu\vdash r-1$ with $\mu$ $\ell$-restricted, $$[L_n(\lambda)^1:L_{n-1}(\mu)]  =[\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}:D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}].$$ The exact functor transfers these surviving multiplicities; it may kill nonrestricted simple factors. At $q=1$ these statements hold over every field for the group algebras. In ordinary James labels the dictionary is $D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$, not an untwisted identification with $D^\lambda$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The field, parameter, ranks, polynomial weight decomposition, and q-Schur and Hecke algebras of the Statement.

[F1] The permutation-summand realization is $S(n,r)=\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(\bigoplus_\alpha M^\alpha)$, with weight projections $1_\alpha$. The regular summand for a composition with exactly $r$ entries equal to $1$ is $M^\alpha=H(r)$. The standard corner is $\omega=(1^r,0^{n-r})$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]], [[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]]).

[F2] The exact Schur functor sends $W^\mu$ to $S_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ and $L_n(\mu)$ to $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$, allowing zero images. The image $D_{\mathrm M}^\mu$ is nonzero if and only if $\mu$ is restricted over the original field; the nonzero images are pairwise nonisomorphic simple modules ([[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F3] Brundan, full author manuscript, §3.22 defines polynomial levels by last-coordinate weight, using both $K_n$ and its binomial operators so the integer weight is determined even at a root of unity. The Levi $U(n-1)$ commutes with these operators. The q-Schur polynomial realization is the corresponding finite-degree quotient. In §5.5 the functors are left-module functors; star converts the right-module suppliers to this convention.

[F4] Every Schur simple $L(\mu)$ is its nonzero cell-form quotient, so the descended symmetric associative form makes $L(\mu)^\circ\cong L(\mu)$ under Schur star. The normalized maps are $\varphi_{ST}(x_\nu h)=m_{ST}h$, with $m_{ST}\in x_\mu H\cap Hx_\nu$ and $m_{TS}=m_{ST}^*$; Schur star is $\varphi_{ST}^*=\varphi_{TS}$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The standard coefficient trace satisfies $\tau(ab)=\tau(ba)$ and $\tau(T_u^*T_v)=\delta_{uv}q^{\ell(u)}$; its complete generator-block proof is the actual standalone trace construction of [[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]] and [[thm-standard-basis-of-the-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]. The following proof establishes the restricted-socle conclusion locally over the original field; no quantum-hyperalgebra square-root or unproved classical-specialization premise is used.

[F5] At $q=1$ the actual ordinary polytabloid/signed-conjugate Murphy comparison gives the group module dictionary, with form factor $1$, over every field. It follows through the corrected Definition and the actual NEW50 comparison and specialization suppliers, not the printed-page-25 untwisted warning ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]]).



## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Construct the lower-rank action directly over the given field. Put $M_0=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Lambda(n-1,r-1)}M^\alpha$ for $H(r-1)$. Length-additive parabolic coset bases give $M^{(\alpha,1)}\cong M^\alpha\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ by $x_\alpha h\otimes a\mapsto x_\alpha ha$. Thus the summands with last coordinate $1$ form $M_1\cong M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$. The functorial algebra homomorphism $f\mapsto f\otimes1$ embeds $S(n-1,r-1)$ into $\operatorname{End}_{H(r)}(M_1)$: the Hecke algebra $H(r)$ is free on its parabolic coset basis and contains the unit coset, so the map is injective. Extend these maps by zero to the remaining summands of $M$ and put $p=\sum_{\alpha_n=1}1_\alpha$. For every left $S(n,r)$-module $V$, $V^1=pV$ is therefore a natural $S(n-1,r-1)$-module. This supplies the lower-rank action without assuming that the first level is a sum of root-adjacent highest-weight spaces, and without adjoining a square root of the Hecke parameter. It agrees with the last-coordinate polynomial level of [F3]. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Prove the Hom assertion algebraically. For $S=S(n,r)$ put $\overline W=Se\otimes_{eSe}eW$ and let $\varepsilon:\overline W\to W$ send $se\otimes w$ to $sw$. Its image is $SeW=W^{(e)}$, which is $W$ under the stated hypothesis. Applying $e$ identifies $e\varepsilon$ with the isomorphism $eSe\otimes_{eSe}eW\to eW$. Exactness of $e(-)$ therefore gives $eK=0$ for $K=\ker\varepsilon$. The exact sequence is $$0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow\overline W   \xrightarrow{\varepsilon}W\longrightarrow0.$$ For any $S$-map $g:\overline W\to V$, its image $g(K)$ is an $S$-submodule killed by $e$, so it is contained in $V_{(e)}=0$. Thus $g$ factors uniquely through $W$. The adjunction then gives $\operatorname{Hom}_H(eW,eV)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(\overline W,V) \cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(W,V)$. This proves assertion 2, with the kernel and quotient in the correct direction. [given, F1]

2.1 Reconcile the corners for all $n\ge r$. Put $\omega_*=(1^{r-1},0^{n-r},1)$ and $e_*=1_{\omega_*}$. Both $M^\omega$ and $M^{\omega_*}$ are the regular module $H(r)$. Their fixed identity isomorphism gives block matrix units $u,v\in S(n,r)$ with $u=e_*ue$, $v=eve_*$, $uv=e_*$ and $vu=e$. Thus multiplication by $u$ gives a natural isomorphism $eV\to e_*V$, with inverse multiplication by $v$, and carries the standard regular corner action to the $e_*$ corner action. When $n=r$ these corners coincide. This explicitly supplies the natural corner identification instead of treating an idempotent with last coordinate $0$ as lying in the first level. [F1, step 1.1]

2.2 Construct a perfect Schur-contravariant form on the permutation-summand module $M$. On each distinguished coset basis $b_d=x_\alpha T_d$, put $\beta_\alpha(b_d,b_c)=\delta_{dc}q^{\ell(d)}$. The row generator cases are a same-row scalar $q$, or an adjacent length-increasing pair with $b_dT_i=b_c$ and $b_cT_i=q b_d+(q-1)b_c$, $\ell(c)=\ell(d)+1$. Their weighted diagonal matrices verify $\beta_\alpha(aT_i,b)=\beta_\alpha(a,bT_i)$, so the forms are Hecke-contravariant and perfect. To prove Schur adjointness, work first in $A=\mathbb Z[Q,Q^{-1}]$. Length-additive cosets and [F4] give $\tau(a^*b)=P_\alpha(Q)\beta_\alpha(a,b)$ on $M_\alpha$, where $P_\alpha=\sum_{u\in S_\alpha}Q^{\ell(u)}$ is nonzero in $A$ with constant coefficient $1$. For $f=\varphi_{ST}:M_\nu\to M_\mu$, $a=x_\nu h$ and $b=x_\mu k$, membership in [F4] gives $m_{TS}x_\mu=P_\mu m_{TS}$ and $x_\nu m_{TS}=P_\nu m_{TS}$. Thus $$P_\mu\beta_\mu(fa,b)=\tau(h^*m_{TS}x_\mu k)=P_\mu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k),\qquad P_\nu\beta_\nu(a,f^*b)=\tau(h^*x_\nu m_{TS}k)=P_\nu\tau(h^*m_{TS}k).$$ Cancel the nonzero polynomials only in $A$, then specialize the resulting identity to $F$. The orthogonal sum $\beta=\bigoplus_\alpha\beta_\alpha$ is therefore perfect and satisfies $\beta(sm,m')=\beta(m,s^*m')$ for every actual Schur basis map and hence every $s\in S$. It identifies the left $S$-module $M$ with $M^\circ$. No Poincare factor is canceled in the given field, including at $q=1$. [F1, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Compute the first-level corner inside this induced action. The lower regular summand is $H(r-1)$, whose induction is $H(r-1)\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)=H(r)$, exactly the summand of type $\omega_*$. Its weight projection on $pV$ is $e_*$, so $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)=e_*V$. The lower corner operator given by left multiplication by $h\in H(r-1)$ induces left multiplication by the same $h$ on $H(r)$ under $a\otimes b\mapsto ab$. Thus every generator $T_1,\ldots,T_{r-2}$ acts exactly as its image in the upper regular corner, by equality of these explicit endomorphisms. The matrix units of step 2.1 identify the upper standard corner with this regular summand. They consequently give $f_{n-1,r-1}(V^1)\cong\operatorname{Res}f_{n,r}(V)$ on every module. This is an algebra-level calculation; it needs no generic semisimplicity or cellular/crystal label identification. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1]

3.2 Determine the simple socle labels of $M$. Evaluation at $1$ in the regular summand gives $Se=\operatorname{Hom}_H(H,M)\cong M$ as a left $S$-module. Finite-dimensional star duality and [F4], together with step 2.2, give $$\operatorname{Hom}_S(L,M)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(M^\circ,L^\circ)\cong\operatorname{Hom}_S(Se,L)\cong eL$$ for every simple $L$. The last bijection evaluates a map at $e$, with inverse $v\mapsto(se\mapsto sv)$ for $v\in eL$. By [F2], $eL(\mu)$ is nonzero exactly for restricted $\mu$. Thus every simple submodule of $M$ has restricted label; for restricted $\lambda$, any nonzero map $L(\lambda)\to M$ is injective. The proof does not equate zero form quotients with zero actual module heads. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.2, algebra]


4.1 Transfer composition multiplicities by exactness, not by a Hom-space count. Apply $f_{n-1,r-1}$ to a finite composition series of $L_n(\lambda)^1$. By [F2] its factors become either zero or the pairwise nonisomorphic $D_{\mathrm M}^{\mu}$ for restricted $\mu$. Removing repeated terms of the resulting filtration therefore preserves the number of each surviving simple factor. Step 3.1 identifies its result with $\operatorname{Res}D_{\mathrm M}^{\lambda}$, proving the stated equality. Assertion 3 is not used to claim that every composition factor survives; a socle statement alone would not justify that claim. [F2, step 3.1]

4.2 Prove the restricted-socle assertion over every original field. Applying $p$ to the injection $L_n(\lambda)\to M$ of step 3.2 embeds $L_n(\lambda)^1$ into $pM=M_1=M_0\otimes_{H(r-1)}H(r)$ with the actual lower action of step 1.1. The length-additive parabolic coset basis makes $H(r)$ free as a LEFT $H(r-1)$-module of rank $r$, so $M_1$ is $r$ copies of $M_0$ as a left lower Schur module. Apply steps 2.2 and 3.2 to $M_0\cong S(n-1,r-1)e_{\rm lower}$: its simple socle labels are exactly the surviving restricted labels. Every simple submodule of $L_n(\lambda)^1$ is a simple submodule of $M_1$, and therefore restricted. At degree zero $M_0=F$, with the unique empty label; at $n=r=1$ this is the convention $S(0,0)=F$. This proves assertion3, without adjoining a square root, using a splitting extension, assuming a quantum-hyperalgebra specialization, or requiring $\lambda_n=0$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.2, algebra]


5.1 At $q=1$, [F5] identifies the corner algebras with group algebras. In ordinary regular labels the two modules are simultaneously twisted by sign and both partition labels are conjugated. Sign restricts along the group tower, is exact, and preserves the two compared multiplicities. This is the ordinary group interpretation, including characteristic $2$; it is not an untwisted identification of a restricted label with the same regular label. Steps 3.1, 1.2, 4.2 and 4.1 prove all the assertions. [F5, step 3.1, step 1.2, step 4.2, step 4.1] ∎

## Remarks

The first-level and ordinary-label reconciliation above is the new authored binding repair. The previously accepted source20 cell-form repair and NEW50 ordinary polytabloid construction are unchanged. Actual acceptance requires the repaired current source20/NEW50 supplier carriers after the live writers drain and the same reviewer checks the actual bound interfaces. No further primitive bridge construction is claimed. No identification of cellular and crystal simple labels is used ([[rem-the-crystal-identification-does-not-elementarily-identify-cellular-simple-labels]]).
